news.title: Controversial AI data centres 'could add £300 a year to Scottish fuel bills'
news.text: Thirty hyperscale AI data centres planned for Scotland could raise household energy bills by over £300 a year it has been warned. Researchers from the Scottish Greens calculate the controversial schemes will require so much power they would raise wholesale electricity prices across the UK due to increased demand on the grid. A Sunday Mail investigation has also uncovered a briefing from the Scottish Parliament’s own research centre which reveals just one of the proposed developments - the 600MW monster site in Auchtertool, Fife - would consume the same energy as 1.6million households. Government agency Scottish Enterprise last week also warned of “massive energy demands” that could “stress Scotland’s electricity system” if construction went ahead without co-ordinated planning and controls. It comes as Scots are already facing an eye-watering 26 per cent hike in average household fuel bills of £443 annually from January driven by conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine. Yet a clutch of data centres in Scotland’s so-called AI Growth Zone are in line for energy discounts worth millions under a Treasury scheme, while being propped up nearly a quarter of a billion pounds in additional public money. That’s despite a key US big tech partner in the project in Chapelhall, Lanarkshire , tanking in value by over 50 per cent in two months amid fears the AI bubble has popped, sending global markets into freefall. Greens MSP Patrick Harvie, said: “Households should not be forced to pay higher energy bills to support the profits of tech giants and billionaires. “The impact of these centres would be massive, not just on our environment but on Scottish households’ electricity bills, in the middle of a cost of living crisis. “We know that hyperscale data centres will put huge pressure on our energy grid and renewable energy supplies. The Scottish Government cannot continue to bury its head in the sand about the impact that these proposals will have on our electricity bills and our natural environment." His party’s research claims that if all 30 proposed hyperscale centres in Scotland went ahead it would raise average energy bills by £317. The figures are based on average bills since 2024, with the likely price impact resulting from an expected extra electricity demand of 9.7GW from proposed data centres calculated on top of this baseline using National Energy System Operator (NESO) data. Dozens of monster data centres to help power big tech and AI models have been proposed across Scotland, although not all are in the planning system yet. The plans have met huge resistance from affected communities amid fears they will cause energy and water shortages and environmental damage while powering AI systems that could put millions of people globally out of work. Campaigners have also warned there will be minimal local job creation or economic benefit after the initial construction phase. Our investigation also found taxpayers are on the hook for £237million in public backing to the AI Growth Zone project in Lanarkshire, which was pledged in August even though financial concerns around the AI sector were already widespread. This consisted of a £202million loan guarantee from the UK Government’s National Wealth Fund and £35million from the Scottish Government-backed Scottish National Investment Bank (SNIB). US AI giant CoreWeave, headquartered in New Jersey, won a lucrative 15-year contract with Airdrie-based DataVita to operate two data centres at the Chapelhall campus last year, pledging to invest £1.5billion of its own money. Tech billionaire CEO Michael Intrator hailed the “state-of-the-art” scheme which was announced during Donald Trump’s second state visit to the UK in September 2025. But since September, the firm’s share price has slid from a high of £76 in September to around £31 today as tech firms on Wall Street have faced a battering. The sell-off has wiped trillions from the global stock market with investors spooked about the viability of the build-out of AI data centres worldwide. Analysts also have specific concerns over CoreWeave’s debts which rocketed from £14billion to around £50billion in the last year and left the firm with a junk credit rating. In July, a month before the loans and loan guarantees from the public purse were announced, CoreWeave went to the leveraged-loan market to raise around £2billion through junk-grade bonds. Dr Kat Jones, director of Action to Protect Rural Scotland (APRS), warned the investment by taxpayers could be at risk if CoreWeave’s financial situation declines further and they cannot fulfil their contract. It comes after global tech titan Microsoft pulled out of a data centre deal in Essex last month. Elsewhere, it was revealed last week a £7million Scottish taxpayer loan to shamed tycoon Sanjeev Gupta's Dalzell steelworks was rolled into a separate data centre venture. Dr Jones told the Sunday Mail : “Just as AI and tech stocks are plunging around the world, and the AI bubble seems about to burst, it is public money, in the form of loans and loan guarantees, which is on the line. “It was obvious months ago that CoreWeave was in a dire financial situation, and the Scottish Government and UK Government should not be risking over £200million of public funds. “As usual, it looks like it will be the public purse that will be left carrying the can if things fall apart. Our governments should not be giving public money, in the form of loans and electricity subsidies , to hyperscale data centres.” We told in September how if all data centres planned in Lanarkshire’s £8.2billion AI Growth Zone are built, they could get an astonishing £80million a year off their energy bills as part of a Westminster discount scheme. Across Scotland, at least 24 data centres are now in the planning system, which if all built would have energy needs nearly twice that of Scotland’s entire peak winter electricity demand. Grassroots campaign groups have sprung up around the country over energy and environmental concerns due to the scale of the projects. The Auchtertool site , for example, would be the size of 40 football pitches. Thousands gathered in Edinburgh last weekend to protest against the controversial AI boom. Another massive data centre at a former nuclear site in Dumfries and Galloway has generated the most public representations ever for the local council, with more than 10,000 people writing in. SNP ministers have vowed to roll out new national planning guidance on large data centres by Christmas amid mounting pressure from campaigners for a total freeze. It follows a transparency row over a Scottish Enterprise report on data centres being circulated among civil servants as early as March but only made public last week. The paper, written for the government agency by Frazer-Nash Consultancy, warned: “Rapid hyperscale expansion could stress Scotland’s electricity system without coordinated planning, data transparency, and targeted mitigations.” An email released under freedom of information from a senior Scottish Government civil servant in March, discussing the report, said: “There is a clear risk here that locals bear the brunt of increased electricity prices- or even a shortage of energy, or unreliable power- while seeing little direct benefit.” But First Minister John Swinney has resisted calls for a moratorium on the schemes, while SNP innovation minister Alyn Smith said this month Scots should embrace data centres as the “whisky bonds of the AI sector”. news.summary: Warning proposed hyperscale schemes would send energy prices soaring while US big tech-backed data centres rake in taxpayer subsidies.

news.title: Trump Steps Out in Bizarre Tribute to His Favorite President
news.text:
In a Reuters photograph, Trump could be seen striking a nearly identical pose to the one on the shirt as he prepared to depart the White House. 

He completed the look with dark navy blue slacks and white shoes.

Another photo, showing Trump posing with a boy at Trump National Golf Club in Sterling, Virginia, offered a closer look at the presidential portrait.

“President Donald J Trump today at Trump National Golf Club Washington DC! HAPPY THANKSGIVING!” MAGA social media booster Michael Solakiewicz posted. 

Internet sleuths quickly set about tracking down the source of Trump’s self-portrait sweatshirt.

Several X users found a similar sweatshirt for sale online, although its depiction of Trump appeared slightly different.

The version available online was arguably less flattering, featuring a few extra wrinkles that Trump’s own sweatshirt had conveniently left out.

Trump spent Saturday morning inspecting construction on his controversial White House ballroom on the site of the East Wing, which he abruptly demolished.

He then headed to his golf club with longtime aide and executive assistant Natalie Harp, 35, in tow. 

The demands of the presidency have done little to curb Trump’s appetite for golf since he returned to the White House in January 2025.

He has spent many weekends on the links in 2026, even as his administration waged war in Iran and he crisscrossed the country campaigning for Republican candidates ahead of the midterms—many of whom ultimately lost.

His love of the game has also sparked a bitter dispute over the East Potomac public golf course in Washington, D.C., which Trump wants to close and overhaul. A Joe Biden-appointed judge has temporarily blocked the project amid an ongoing legal battle. 

The White House did not immediately respond to questions about why Trump was wearing his own likeness—or where he got the sweatshirt.
news.summary:
Ken Cedeno / REUTERSPresident Donald Trump turned his Saturday golf outing into a one-man fan club meeting, sporting an outfit that paid tribute to a very familiar face.

The president, 80, was spotted at his Sterling, Virginia, golf club wearing an oversized white sweatshirt emblazoned with a sketch of his own face—complete with his signature pointing finger.

In a Reuters photograph, Trump could be seen striking a nearly identical pose to the one on the shirt as he prepared to depart the White House. 

Read more at The Daily Beast.
news.author: Sarah-Jane Collins

news.title: Report: Trump Favors Economic Stranglehold on Iran Over Renewed Major Strikes
news.text:
President Donald Trump reportedly favors intensifying the economic campaign against Iran over renewed major military strikes, with Washington seeking to choke off the regime’s remaining oil-export routes as Tehran struggles under the weight of the American blockade.

Trump currently favors expanding the economic campaign among four options presented by his advisers, according to a Saturday report by Israel Hayom citing three diplomatic sources familiar with the deliberations. The strategy reportedly includes pressing Gulf governments to help shut down Iranian oil-smuggling routes through Iraq while maintaining the naval blockade and expanding efforts to protect commercial shipping from Iranian attacks.

The reported preference comes as Trump resists calls for another major offensive, Iranian forces threaten to break the blockade, and diplomatic efforts remain deadlocked over Tehran’s nuclear program and control of the Strait of Hormuz.

The administration weighed four approaches: negotiating an agreement with Tehran, launching another major offensive, conducting limited strikes against Iranian nuclear and military facilities, or intensifying the economic campaign, the report said.

Negotiations have stalled over Tehran’s refusal to accept Washington’s terms, while another major offensive risks triggering widespread Iranian retaliation against American forces and Gulf infrastructure without guaranteeing a decisive result, according to the report. Limited strikes remain under consideration, but Trump reportedly favors tightening the economic squeeze, with support from Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

Trump has repeatedly signaled his reluctance to resume major strikes, previously describing another offensive as “highly unlikely” and more recently indicating that he is in no rush to make a decision. Rubio has likewise argued that Washington is achieving its objectives through economic pressure without another major military campaign.

The administration had already begun extending its interdiction efforts beyond Iranian ports, with CENTCOM announcing Task Force Iron Gate two weeks ago to disrupt illicit revenue, weapons shipments, and sanctioned materials moving across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea.

The latest effort reportedly focuses on Iranian crude moving through Iraq, where shipments are disguised as Iraqi or Kurdish oil before being routed toward ports in Syria or Turkey. Washington is pressing Gulf governments to help shut down the trade, and regional leaders have reportedly pledged to pressure Baghdad to cooperate, according to the Israeli report.

CENTCOM marked 130 consecutive days of the naval blockade Saturday, crediting American forces with preventing the IRGC from exporting billions of dollars in crude oil. The command previously estimated that the blockade had prevented more than $25 billion in Iranian crude exports.

The financial squeeze intensified Friday when the Treasury Department sanctioned four Iranian oil trustees accused of handling proceeds from the regime’s crude sales, including intermediaries who allegedly pocketed money intended for Tehran. The sanctions are part of Operation Economic Outcast, the broader campaign launched in August to cut off the regime’s remaining financial lifelines.

Treasury said Iran had not loaded oil onto vessels since the campaign began and had no crude aboard ships outside the American blockade, leaving Tehran scrambling to recover billions of dollars from oil already sold.

Bessent, who reportedly relocated to a military installation after Iranian death threats against him reached an advanced stage, warned during a Friday evening Newsmax interview that mounting economic pressure could soon trigger infighting within Tehran’s leadership.

“I regard the bounty that they have on my head as a sign of success,” Bessent said.

“My guess is they will soon start turning on each other,” he predicted. “They may start lashing out in terms of some indiscriminate shooting in the Middle East, but they are wounded, cornered animals.”

Bessent said the campaign could ultimately bring Tehran to the negotiating table or deepen divisions within the IRGC.

Iran’s own president has acknowledged the worsening economic crisis, including severe energy shortages threatening industrial production.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian described the country’s predicament Saturday as a “silent economic war,” warning that its effects could prove more difficult to endure than the destruction caused by missile strikes.

Pezeshkian acknowledged that gas shortages predated attacks on Iranian facilities and urged officials to shield factories from electricity cuts, warning that further disruptions could threaten jobs and deepen the economic crisis.

Rather than soften its negotiating demands, Tehran has threatened to confront the American blockade directly.

Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi warned Saturday that Tehran would take whatever measures it considered necessary to break the blockade, which he characterized as an act of war.

“We will take whatever measures necessary to break it,” he declared, according to Iranian state broadcaster Press TV.

The warning comes as more than a dozen Iranian oil tankers have reportedly gathered near Kharg Island, the country’s principal crude-export terminal, amid discussions in Iranian media of a convoy intended to challenge the blockade.

Iranian sources have also threatened attacks on energy infrastructure in neighboring Gulf states if American forces intercept the vessels. The proposed convoy has not been confirmed to have departed, and there is no verified indication that it has breached the blockade.

The warnings come amid another round of attacks on Gulf shipping and infrastructure, underscoring the risks of escalation as Washington tightens its economic campaign.

Two commercial tankers were struck by projectiles near the Strait of Hormuz Saturday, with one reporting damage to its stern and another to its engine room, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency. No casualties were reported.

Bahrain also reported an Iranian attack on a civilian industrial facility Saturday that sparked a fire and caused material damage but no casualties. The IRGC separately claimed strikes against American air-defense radar systems at Al-Riffa and Awali.

The latest claims follow earlier Iranian assertions that its drones struck American radar installations in Bahrain last Friday and again Tuesday. Although Tehran has repeatedly claimed to have damaged American military equipment, those claims remain unverified, with a U.S. official reporting no damage to American forces or military assets in the latest attacks.

Tehran has also sought to project military strength despite the damage inflicted on its forces during American and Israeli operations.

On Saturday, IRGC commander Ahmad Vahidi toured an underground missile facility showcased by Iranian state media, where commanders displayed a purported dual-missile launcher and threatened further retaliation against their adversaries.

Gulf governments, meanwhile, are seeking stronger protection for oil facilities, gas infrastructure, and desalination plants amid Iranian attacks, including expanded defensive coordination with Israel, according to the Israeli report. Regional leaders have also expressed concern that another major American offensive could expose their countries to further Iranian retaliation.

Even as the military confrontation intensifies, diplomatic channels remain open, though Tehran has shown little willingness to retreat from the demands Washington has rejected.

Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Qatari mediators in Berlin Thursday, followed by a Qatari delegation’s visit to Tehran Friday. The discussions produced no announced breakthrough.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi insisted Saturday that Tehran would not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until Washington accepted its conditions, including lifting the American blockade.

“There is no solution to the current situation unless the US acknowledges its mistakes and fulfills its previous commitments,” Araghchi declared, according to Press TV.

Gharibabadi separately claimed Iran could reopen the waterway within hours if Washington lifted the blockade and released frozen Iranian funds. He also ruled out transferring Tehran’s enriched uranium stockpile abroad under a potential agreement.

Those demands remain incompatible with Trump’s insistence on a lasting agreement that permanently prevents Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons.

Speaking to reporters Friday, Trump accused Tehran of seeking another agreement that would leave its nuclear ambitions unresolved.

“They want to make a deal, but they don’t want to make a deal that’s acceptable to me,” Trump said. “We want to make a real deal, not a fake deal that they’ve been doing for 51 years.”

“They’ve been bullshitting people for 51 years,” he added.

Trump sharpened that demand Saturday, telling Fox News that any agreement must endure beyond his presidency and prevent future administrations from allowing Iran to acquire nuclear weapons.

“I’m going to make a deal that is going to be permanent,” he said. “I’m not going to let somebody allow them to have a nuclear weapon.”

Trump’s reported preference leaves the threat of renewed military strikes on the table while seeking to deprive Tehran of the oil revenues sustaining its regime — a strategy aimed at forcing an agreement that Iranian leaders continue to resist, even as they threaten to break the blockade by force.
news.summary:
President Donald Trump reportedly favors intensifying the economic campaign against Iran over renewed major military strikes, with Washington seeking to choke off the regime’s remaining oil-export routes as Tehran struggles under the weight of the American blockade.


The post Report: Trump Favors Economic Stranglehold on Iran Over Renewed Major Strikes appeared first on Breitbart.

news.title: Trump Orders Contractors To Consult White House Before Responding To Congress
news.text: President Donald Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged, according to a new executive order.The companies must also coordinate with the White House and US agencies on "appropriate responses" to any such requests, the order issued late Friday says. If they fail to comply, the White House warns their contracts could be terminated and their future work with the federal government suspended.The order is the Republican administration's latest effort to resist what are expected to be wide-ranging and aggressive oversight efforts from Democrats when they take over Congress in January. Democrats have made government contracts one of their top investigative targets, noting that federal money has been flowing to companies linked with Trump's family, particularly at the Pentagon.White House officials have already begun taking steps to exert more control over how agencies and officials respond to congressional requests, anticipating there will be a flood of investigations initiated by Democrats.Trump's counsel, Will Scharf, told federal agencies on Monday that they must seek approval from his office and the White House's Office of Legislative Affairs before agreeing to appear before Congress. Scharf also suggested in a recent letter to Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, that some congressional investigations may amount to "blatant criminality."Garcia sent letters this week directing members of Trump's family and top administration officials to preserve documents. Scharf sought to dismiss the requests, noting in a letter to Democratic lawmakers that they are not yet in the majority and cannot compel compliance.Responding to the new executive order, Garcia said Saturday it was part of the administration's "blatant attack on Congress' constitutional right to conduct oversight." He said that despite efforts to impede investigations, "we're just getting started."Rep. Jamie Raskin, the leader of Democratic investigations from the House Judiciary Committee, slammed Trump's order as "totally unprecedented and blatantly unlawful." He said public contractors have a "duty and a right to speak truthfully when Congress calls."In a fact sheet, the White House framed the new requirements as "protecting executive privileges from congressional overreach," arguing that some congressional leaders have tried to intrude on executive branch privileges by "harassing private companies that contract with the federal government."Presidents of both parties have long used executive privilege to resist congressional inquiries, but the claims can set up messy, protracted legal fights as parties dispute whether it applies. Executive privilege allows the president to keep information from the courts, Congress and the public to protect the confidentiality of White House deliberations, but the protection is far from absolute.The latest executive order applies to all contractors and subcontractors, a universe of tens of thousands of businesses.(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)
news.summary: The order is the Republican administration's latest effort to resist what are expected to be wide-ranging and aggressive oversight efforts from Democrats when they take over Congress in January.
news.author: Associated Press

news.title: Fresh legal probe into Nvidia raises the stakes for the world’s biggest chipmaker
news.text:
California’s probe into whether Nvidia illegally sold advanced chips to China and misled investors about the conduct is also looking at potential criminal violations of state law, raising the stakes for the chipmaker.

The state’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, said late last week that there are a variety of California laws that could have been broken if Nvidia or former chief executive Jensen Huang gave false information to the public about such sales.

The investigation is in a preliminary stage and has not led to any conclusions.

“The basic legal framework that we’re looking at is the prohibitions in California law — both civil and criminal — against misleading investors and the public,” Mr Bonta said.

“And there are multiple different laws that provide prohibitions in that space.”

Mr Bonta’s investigation was triggered in part by revelations that Huang had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who worked at a Singapore-based firm that obtained advanced chips from his company.

The scandal plunged Nvidia into an unprecedented crisis, fueling a sharp selloff in the company’s shares and resulting in Huang’s ouster as CEO.

The United States government is looking into several aspects of Nvidia’s conduct.

US President Donald Trump said the FBI is looking into Huang’s relationship with the suspected spy, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the company’s own probe will help determine whether it was “promiscuous” in terms of sales of high-end chips that were likely to end up in China.

“I think we’re gonna find out as the company does their investigation what was really going on,” Mr Bessent said.

The Nvidia revelations also raised “very bright red flags” for Mr Bonta’s office, he said.

If an investigation concludes Nvidia violated the law, Mr Bonta said, the penalties could include a court order barring further violations and the return of any profit from illegal sales, which could be substantial.

Mr Bonta added that if any violations are uncovered, the probe has the potential to lead to a criminal case against Nvidia, which could also result in financial penalties.

Nvidia is the world’s largest chipmaker and was, until recently, the world’s most valuable publicly traded company. Under Huang’s leadership its products became central to the massive build-out in artificial intelligence infrastructure.
news.summary: California’s probe into whether Nvidia illegally sold advanced chips to China and misled investors about the conduct is also looking at potential criminal violations of state law.
news.author: Erik Larson

news.title: Taiwan warns Canada’s Carney that deeper ties with China come with risks
news.text: HALIFAX: Taiwan's deputy foreign minister warned on Saturday that Prime Minister Mark Carney risks exposing Canada to the very economic coercion he has cautioned against by deepening trade ties with China, saying that Taiwan has learned the hard way that dependence on Beijing comes with consequences."We worry. We worry," Chen Ming-chi told The Associated Press in an interview at the Halifax International Security Forum when asked about Carney's efforts to improve relations with China.Carney has warned that major powers are using economic integration as a weapon, citing U.S. tariffs and China's restrictions on critical minerals. He has urged middle powers to diversify their trade relationships to avoid economic coercion.Chen praised Carney's speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, but questioned whether Canada should deepen ties with countries that don't share its democratic values."Who do you want to choose as your partners?" he asked."You have your own history. You have two Michaels," Chen said, referring to former Canadian diplomat Michael Kovrig and businessman Michael Spavor, whose ne arly three-year detention in China prompted accusations of hostage diplomacy..Carney says Canada’s growing trade ties with China are not a top concern for Trump.The two were arrested in 2018 shortly after Canada detained Huawei executive Meng Wanzhou on a U.S. extradition request. They were released in September 2021, the same day Meng returned to China. Beijing denied their detention was politically motivated.Chen's warning came days after Carney met with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen and agreed to additional tariff reductions as Canada seeks to diversify trade during U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war.Carney said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if negotiations with Washington fail to preserve a viable Canadian auto industry. Trump has threatened 50% tariffs on Canadian vehicles and auto parts beginning on Jan. 1.Chen warned that Chinese electric vehicles could threaten Canadian manufacturers and pose surveillance risks because of their connected technology, even if manufactured in Canada.Carney has argued that Canada's trade relationship with China differs from Washington's more complicated ties with Beijing. Canada primarily exports agricultural products, energy and other commodities rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.Chen said that Taiwan had dramatically reduced its economic dependence on China after experiencing Beijing's use of trade restrictions to exert political pressure..Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail."They are very good at weaponizing interdependence," he said. "They are very good at leveraging our dependence to reach political goals."Taiwan reduced the share of its outbound investment going to China from more than 80% in 2010 to 3.8% last year, Chen said. Its exports to China and Hong Kong fell from nearly 44% of total exports in 2020 to about 27% last year, according to Taiwanese government figures.Chen also accused Beijing of exploiting a striking photograph from this week's summit in Shenzhen showing Xi seated prominently between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin to project China as the world's leading power."The main idea is to prove not only to his domestic audience that he is the world leader," Chen said. "They are so good at propaganda."He described the summit as "more symbolic than substantial."Chen said China was intensifying military operations around Taiwan, despite the potentially enormous costs of an invasion. He warned that Chinese vessels could be rehearsing for a maritime quarantine of the self-governing island.Despite his concerns about Beijing, Chen praised Carney's international leadership and welcomed his commitment to sign a long-delayed trade cooperation arrangement with Taiwan."We have a high respect of Prime Minister Carney's vision. And we want to be part of this vision," he said..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy has a message for Americans opposing data centres
news.text: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy has said it would be a "historic mistake" for the US to pull back on building AI data centres, just weeks after a midterm election in which voters turned against the facilities in large numbers. Speaking at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World event, Jassy argued that slowing down now would hand China the chance to set the rules for artificial intelligence."I cannot fathom any scenario where the United States stops building data centres and allows another country like China to establish all the norms," Jassy said, as reported by Semafor. He added that the US would regret such a move "for a very long time."Jassy did not brush the backlash aside, though. He acknowledged that tech companies need to "do it better and partner more closely with our communities."Amazon plans to spend around $220 billion on AI infrastructure this yearFew executives have more riding on the AI buildout than Jassy, who has directed hundreds of billions of dollars into data centres around the world. He reaffirmed that Amazon's capital expenditure will be around $220 billion this year and "meaningfully more" next year. He did not share a figure for 2027.In a TV interview after the event, Jassy went a step further. He said it would be a "catastrophic" mistake for the US to fall significantly behind China, and that the country had underinvested in its power grid even before AI came along. He compared the current buildout to the highways and bridges the US built in the 1950s.The White House is making a similar China argument. On Friday, President Donald Trump threatened a "tremendous tax" on American companies that build AI data centres outside the country. "We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," he told reporters, adding that the US could fall behind China if the backlash slows construction at home. Trump said he had not yet told his staff about the plan, and it is not clear how it would be enforced. His advice to wary communities was to negotiate with tech companies for tax breaks, lower utility bills and direct payments. "Make them pay you. Make them pay your community," he said.Amazon is also bringing in outside money for some of its facilities. Blackstone's data centre trust has agreed to buy a 75% stake in two joint ventures that hold 13 AWS buildings, in a deal valued at about $5 billion.Voters and newly elected Democrats want new data centre projects pausedThe backlash Jassy and Trump are responding to was one of the defining issues of this month's midterms. Democrats swept the elections, and voters rejected data centre development in nearly all of 41 local ballot measures. In one post-election voter poll, 56% of voters said AI and data centres were a crucial or major factor in how they voted.Several winning Democrats made data centres part of their victory speeches. "I do not work for data centres," Ohio Senator-elect Sherrod Brown told supporters. Senator Bernie Sanders has since called for a national data centre moratorium.The pressure is building at the state level too. Incoming Texas Governor Gina Hinojosa has pledged to halt new data centre approvals until the state passes laws to protect residents. Texas alone is home to 27% of planned data centre capacity in the US, according to Wells Fargo.Public opinion was shifting well before the vote. A Pew Research Center survey conducted between July and August found that 54% of Americans think data centres are mostly bad for the environment, up from 39% in January. Half said they are mostly bad for home energy costs, while 60% said they would be uncomfortable with a new data centre operating in their area.Electricity bills are a big part of that worry. In a separate survey by researchers at Yale and George Mason University, 59% of Americans said they expect their power bills to go up if a data centre opens nearby. Only 15% said they would support one being built in their local area, while 56% said they would oppose it.Fearless legend or grounded realist? news.summary: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy says pulling back on AI data centres would be a "historic mistake" that lets China set the rules for artificial intelligence. Speaking at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World, Jassy reaffirmed Amazon's $220 billion capex plan. His remarks come as President Trump threatens a "tremendous tax" on overseas data centres and Democrats push for moratoriums following the US midterm election backlash.

news.title: Trump reposts Democrat Abdul El-Sayed's TrumpCare proposal
news.text:
President Donald Trump reposted a Democratic senator-elect's universal “TrumpCare” proposal on Truth Social Saturday, after telling Fox News that a health deal with Democrats was possible.

Trump added no caption to the screenshot of Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed's Nov. 12 X post, which put guaranteed healthcare “for every American, from cradle to grave” on the table. Whether the repost signaled support for the proposal was not immediately known.

The post showed mock-ups of a TrumpCare insurance card in gold, a tribute to Trump's favorite color, according to NBC News. Its reverse reads “Show this card at any doctor, hospital clinic, or pharmacy in the United States.” It resembles the $1 million Trump Gold Card offered by the administration to foreigners seeking U.S. residency.

This is a message for @realDonaldTrump. Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.— Dr. Abdul El-Sayed (@AbdulElSayed) November 12, 2026

Before sharing the post, Trump told Fox News in a Saturday morning phone interview that the government could “do tremendous things on healthcare” when Democrats assume control of Congress in January. “I mean, I could sit there for two years and one month and just veto everything, veto everything, and nothing would get done for anyone, and that's not the way to go,” Trump said.

“There's a chance that we can do better than we did where we had a very small majority with the Republicans,” he said.

El-Sayed offered to work with Senate leaders in a statement Saturday afternoon. “If the President is serious about meeting the unmet promise of guaranteed healthcare in this country, I'm ready to work alongside leaders in the Senate like Senators Van Hollen, Sanders, Wyden, and Warren to deliver,” he said. “President Trump, give me a call. I'm happy to chat,” he said.

He had a social media reply for a post about Trump's repost. “Let's get to work, then. Ready when you are @realDonaldTrump,” El-Sayed wrote.

White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster had criticized the proposal before Trump shared it. “The Radical Democrats' socialist proposal for a government takeover of healthcare should really be called 'Medicare for None' as it destroys access to the life-saving care Americans rely on daily,” she told Fox News Digital earlier.

A plan bearing Trump's name

El-Sayed, a former public health official, made Medicare for All central to his campaign and defeated Trump-backed Republican former congressman Mike Rogers in the midterms. The Daily Mail reported that his proposal would provide coverage from birth to death for every American, without premiums, deductibles or copays.

El-Sayed addressed Trump through the camera in an earlier interview with CNN's Kaitlan Collins. “Donald, if you're watching, we can put your name on it,” he said. “I know you like to put your name on stuff. You can finally meet the unmet promise in America to guarantee everybody health care. So it's on the table if you want to do it.”

“But are you being serious or are you being funny?” Collins asked.

“No, I'm absolutely serious,” El-Sayed said earlier.

Deal talk and veto threats

Trump had expressed openness to a healthcare deal at a White House news conference Friday. “Can it be what they want? No. But it can be a combination of what we all want,” he said.

“They're going to send things my way and I'm going to veto them,” Trump said at that news conference.

Later on Saturday, Trump posted a Truth Social image of himself in a red “VETO”-branded hat and matching jacket.

“I'll get along, probably, with the Democrats unless they want to be destructive,” Trump said earlier, on the day following the midterm election. He said at the time that he had veto power.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, chosen as the next speaker, said Nov. 18 that lowering health care costs would be among his party's first priorities. “Out of the gate, what we clearly have to do is fix our broken health care system,” Jeffries said.

news.summary: The Michigan senator-elect offered to work with Senate leaders after Trump reposted his proposal without a caption.

news.title: Trump says US govt to penalise firms building data centres abroad
news.text: President Donald Trump said on Friday that the US would penalise American companies that build data centres overseas, a move he said is intended to help the US artificial intelligence sector compete with its Chinese counterparts. "We're not going to ‌allow our companies to build data centres ​outside of our country," Trump ​said while discussing AI at a White House news conference following ​his trip to Asia. He said he would impose a "tremendous tax" on companies that build data centres abroad. Data centres are critical to the AI boom because they provide the computing power needed to train and run increasingly complex ​AI systems, and a penalty could complicate the global AI buildout. Several major ‌American data centre developers build and operate such facilities outside the ​US, including Equinix and Digital Realty. Data centre developers often locate facilities close to users to reduce delays for time-sensitive tasks such as payment processing. Transmitting large volumes of data ‌over long distances can also ​add significant costs. Trump has been ‌a staunch advocate for data centre construction in the US, a position ‌that is unpopular with voters. Data centres have drawn opposition in communities nationwide over ​concerns about electricity demand, utility costs and other local impacts. The Commerce Department moved on Monday to restrict exports of advanced ​AI chips to several Southeast Asian countries, part of a broader effort to prevent China from obtaining the technology through third ‌countries. The United States already bars direct sales of the most advanced AI ‌chips to China, but Chinese companies have continued to access them by renting computing capacity at data centres in countries that can legally import the chips.
news.summary: Data centres are critical to the AI boom because they provide the computing power needed to train and run increasingly complex ​AI systems, and a penalty could complicate the global AI buildout

news.title: Trump hails Putin and Xi as ‘friends’ again (PHOTOS)
news.text:
US President Donald Trump has posted a series of photographs with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping following their summit in Shenzhen, referring to both leaders as “friends.”

The images were shared on his Truth Social account on Saturday, two days after the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, held in Shenzhen on November 18–19. Trump previously described the gathering as “one of the most momentous international summits in many years,” calling the relationship between the three leaders “fantastic.”

The photographs capture warm interactions between the heads of state. One image shows Trump shaking hands with Putin, accompanied by the caption “My Friend.”

Another shows Xi greeting the US president on the airport tarmac after he disembarked from his plane, similarly captioned “Friends.”

The posts also included several images featuring all three leaders together, including one taken before their trilateral meeting at the Kylin Villa state residence in Shenzhen. Another showed the heads of delegations posing for a group photograph at the APEC summit, bearing the caption “GOAT,” an acronym for “greatest of all time.”

The meeting resulted in what Trump described as a first-of-its-kind trilateral peace declaration, including commitments to reduce nuclear risks and expand dialogue between the three nuclear powers.

The US president said his separate bilateral discussions with Putin focused on ending the Ukraine conflict, with the Russian leader expressing a desire for a diplomatic settlement. He also stressed the importance of maintaining direct communication with Moscow, given Russia’s vast nuclear arsenal.

Meanwhile, Trump’s meeting with Xi was “very productive,” with the two leaders discussing trade, advanced technology, and economic cooperation. He also announced an agreement to develop joint safeguards for advanced artificial intelligence, which he calls “superintelligence.”

Speaking at a White House press conference on Friday, the US president defended his friendly approach toward Moscow and Beijing, dismissing critics of his relations with the Russian and Chinese leaders as “stupid people.”

“I have fantastic relationships with Putin, that’s a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That’s a good thing. And our country is safe because of that,” Trump said.
news.summary:
President Trump has shared photos with Putin and Xi from the APEC summit in China, calling them friends and praising their historic meeting

news.title: Democrats won big in the midterms. Here's what they plan to do next
news.text: Democrats basking in their November 3 election wins will soon unveil an ambitious legislative agenda for the first 100 days and ​beyond, in a test of progressives' influence and Republicans' willingness to cooperate, as they take control of the US Congress on January 3. That agenda is likely to be unveiled in early December once a Senate leadership race is settled. It will mark a thunderous reversal of the past two years, when President Donald Trump's Republicans ruled the Senate and House of Representatives. With their narrow majorities, they rammed through major tax cuts skewed toward the rich and stood by as Trump grabbed their powers over tariffs and spending. Democrats' new majorities in Congress are anything but narrow. With a 56-44 majority in the Senate they are four votes short of the 60 votes needed to advance most legislation. In the House, their 257-172 force could grow beyond an 85-vote margin once a ‌handful of races are settled. "This is a realignment," said Democratic Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia in a post-election ​interview with reporters. But in a warning to Democrats, veteran Republican Senator John Boozman of ​Arkansas said in an interview that despite his party's losses across the United States, Trump remains "a powerful force" and "I don't see any of his vetoes getting overridden" by Congress during his remaining two years in office. AGGRESSIVE AGENDA For ​months, Democrats have been plotting a House-Senate coordinated attack to undo Trump's major accomplishments, according to lawmakers and aides. With the high cost of living the top concern voiced by voters, Democratic leaders are going after the low-hanging fruit that also would help unite their party's progressives and moderates. Early votes are expected on legislation handcuffing Trump's ability to wage war on Iran without Congress' approval, which would help lower gasoline prices. Reversing Republicans' deep cuts to Medicaid and SNAP food stamp programs would begin helping the poor meet healthcare and grocery costs. Meanwhile, progressives have urged raising the federal minimum wage, which is unchanged since 2009 at $7.25 per hour. Some are pushing for $20 to $25. And in response to voter ​disgust over Washington ethics breaches, one of the first bills Democrats are expected to present is one barring lawmakers from insider trading of stocks. Republicans face a bind: joining Democrats could anger Trump unless he backs measures, while stonewalling could anger voters. "I think ‌there's a real understanding in Congress that things like healthcare, the really exorbitant premiums, you know, that people are having to pay" must be addressed, said Boozman, who was one of the Republicans ​who supported around $1 trillion in cuts to Medicare, Medicaid and Obamacare programs enacted last year. Boozman is one of the senators who would be up for re-election in 2028 and potentially open to cooperating with Democrats, although he said he would seek guidance from Trump. 'WE NEED MORE DEMOCRACY' Newly elected progressives, who are growing in numbers in state and local offices, have a far deeper agenda for the next two years such as cutting off aid to Israel and placing a moratorium on new AI data centers. Their ‌to-do list also includes revamping campaign finance rules, raising taxes on the rich, writing comprehensive immigration ​reform and mitigating the effects of climate change. The incoming class of members of Congress averages about eight ‌years younger than now in the House and 14 years younger in the Senate, according to government figures. "We'd have to actually confront monopoly power, whether it's in tech or whether it's in the utility ‌or other major industries," said Democratic Representative-elect William Lawrence, 36, who flipped a Republican-held seat in Michigan. "There's a lot of talk about protecting democracy. We need more democracy in the economy," Lawrence said. Other complex issues, ranging from ​comprehensive immigration reform, and universal healthcare to more aggressive enforcement of environmental laws also populate an already-crowded Democratic wish list. Retiring Democratic Senator Dick Durbin of Illinois said he has talked to colleagues about the need next year to tackle outdated laws governing work visas, the path to citizenship for migrants who lack papers and long-term border security steps, without some ​of the extreme deportation practices of the Trump administration. "With the numbers that we have, we have to try to press forward, try to make a bipartisan 60 votes in the Senate" on comprehensive immigration legislation, Durbin said in a hallway interview. IMMIGRATION, MEDICARE FOR ALL PRIORITIES For years, many Republicans have argued Congress should hold off on sweeping immigration reforms until the southern US border is secured. ‌Trump maintains that he has now accomplished that. In 2013, a bipartisan immigration reform bill passed the Senate by a vote of 68-32, only to be killed by the Republican-controlled House at the time. Meanwhile, moderate Democrats, who outnumber ‌progressives in Congress, have largely shied away from the universal healthcare "Medicare for All" idea progressives demand. But in recent months it has been showing signs of gaining traction with more politicians and voters. Senator Bernie Sanders has a proposal to phase in universal coverage over four years, beginning with lowering the Medicare eligibility age to 55, expanding dental, vision and hearing benefits, and guaranteeing coverage for all children. Democratic Representative Chellie Pingree of Maine, first elected in 2008, expects to chair a House panel overseeing federal environmental spending in January. "I think people are deeply worried about the rollback of clean air, clean water standards, climate change issues, also just the toxins in our environment," Pingree said, hinting at her 2027 subcommittee agenda.
news.summary: Democrats are preparing a sweeping legislative agenda ahead of taking control of both chambers of Congress on January 3

news.title: ICE arrest at Seattle Airport prompts outcry from officials, politicians
news.text: By Michael B. Marois An arrest by federal immigration agents at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport sparked outrage among officials and politicians Saturday, and intensified scrutiny of Immigration and Customs Enforcement as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and investigate the agency’s tactics. Masked federal agents confronted passengers on a jet bridge as they boarded an Alaska Airlines flight to Los Angeles, forcing a woman to the ground in a chaotic encounter captured on video. The confrontation delayed the flight. The Port of Seattle said it was “outraged” by the incident, which involved ICE and two passengers. ICE said its officers were attempting to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, a Mexican national who they said had overstayed his visa, when other passengers interfered with the operation. The agency said a second passenger, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, allegedly threw hot coffee at officers and was also arrested. She will be charged with assaulting a federal officer, according to ICE. Alaska Airlines said in an emailed statement that it had no advance notice of the enforcement action and was working to determine whether proper protocols were followed. The airline said it was concerned by the incident, which it described as distressing for passengers and employees, and emphasized that it doesn’t direct or coordinate immigration enforcement. “I’m outraged by disturbing video of ICE agents forcing a woman to the ground on a jet bridge at SeaTac,” Senator Patty Murray, a Washington Democrat, said in a post on X. “Trump answers to a Democratic Congress on January 3rd — there WILL be accountability.” Democrats are preparing to take control of both chambers of Congress in January, promising investigations into President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown. Lawmakers have identified ICE’s enforcement practices, treatment of detainees and use of federal authority among the targets of planned congressional oversight, which could include hearings, subpoenas and demands for agency records. In October, undercover federal immigration agents arrested a woman at Los Angeles International Airport in another encounter captured on video. Washington Governor Bob Ferguson, also a Democrat, called Saturday’s incident “just the latest example of ICE’s deeply un-American tactics,” saying the agency was “completely and totally out of control.” The Port of Seattle said in a statement that immigration enforcement actions at the airport occur without its participation or knowledge. The Port said it was discussing with the Department of Homeland Security whether previously agreed protocols had been breached and was seeking more information from federal officials.
news.summary: Masked federal agents confronted passengers on a jet bridge as they boarded an Alaska Airlines flight to Los Angeles, forcing a woman to the ground in a chaotic encounter captured on video

news.title: Trump Shares El-Sayed’s ‘TrumpCare’ Plan, Says He May Work with Democrats
news.text: President Donald Trump on Saturday reposted a photo of a gold TrumpCare card proposed by Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed to advance a plan for universal healthcare, as he told Fox News that he might be open to working with Democrats on a plan. The president posted a screenshot of El-Sayed’s X post on his namesake social media platform, Truth Social on Saturday. The screenshot, which was posted without a caption, shows images of a gold TrumpCare and reads “Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.” What Trump said on Fox News Also on Saturday, Trump called into Fox News to talk about how his final two years in office will look under a Democratic majority in Congress. He continued to threaten vetoes, but also said he can see collaboration. "There's a chance that we can do better than we did where we had a very small majority with the Republicans," he said. "They are going to send things, and not all of their things are bad. They have some good points on health care, and they have some bad points, and we have some good things, and probably they would say we have some bad things. But there's a chance we could get great health care and a lot of other things, and we do it in a bipartisan way." Newsweek reached out to the White House via email Saturday for comment on Trump's post on TruthSocial. Trump has also told reporters at a press conference Friday that he is “open to great healthcare” and sees the possibility of getting “a lot of great things done” with a Democrat-controlled Congress. What is TrumpCare? Universal health care has been a core doctrine of Democrat El-Sayed’s politics since he ran for governor of Michigan and lost in 2018. After defeating Republican Mike Rogers in the Michigan Senate race as part of a ‘"blue wave’ that swept the midterms, El-Sayed posted a video on X calling Trump “habibi” and telling him that if he “wanted to be the most popular President in America,” he should implement TrumpCare for All. “You can put your name all over it. You can even give them a gold card,” said El-Sayed. The gold card mock-up features "TrumpCare" in a large font on the front and "Show this card at any doctor, hospital clinic, or pharmacy in the United States" on the back. The design appears similar to the Trump Gold Card, touted to wealthy foreigners seeking a U.S. visa. El-Sayed studied medicine and previously worked with local health departments, according to his campaign website. He wrote "Medicare for All: A Citizen’s Guide," which details a proposal for building a healthcare system that guarantees affordable care for all Americans. While serving as the health director for Wayne County, he helped launch a program that helped erase millions of dollars in medical debt for residents. In 2020, El-Sayed was selected to serve on President Joe Biden's Unity Task Force for Healthcare to help lower prescription drug prices. On his campaign website, El-Sayed describes Medicare for All as covering all necessary healthcare for every single American. He also says he favors getting rid of all medical debt for every American "immediately." Newsweek emailed El-Sayed’s senatorial campaign for further comment via email Saturday. In a social media post Saturday, El-Sayed responded to a post about the president’s TruthSocial declaration, saying “Let’s get to work, then. Ready when you are @realDonaldTrump.” "I mean, I could sit there for two years and one month and just veto everything, veto everything, and nothing would get done for anyone, and that's not the way to go," Trump said during his call with Fox News.
news.summary: President Donald Trump shared a screenshot of Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed's TrumpCare plan on TruthSocial.
news.author: Isabella Paoletto

news.title: Trump opens door to bipartisan deal on credit card rates as Americans face record debt
news.text: President Donald Trump signaled Saturday that he is willing to work with Democrats to cap credit card interest rates at 10%, renewing his push to lower borrowing costs as Americans grapple with record credit card debt. During an interview with Fox News' Kayleigh McEnany on "Saturday in America," Trump was asked whether he could work with Democrats in the next session of Congress to establish a one-year cap. "I would do it," Trump responded. "These credit card companies have made a lot and the credit card fees that they charge, I'm all into it." Trump acknowledged that some critics could view the proposed cap as inconsistent with free-market principles, but argued that consumers should not face excessive fees. AS US CREDIT CARD DEBT HITS $1.29T, BANK ALGORITHMS ARE REJECTING DEBT-FREE, SIX-FIGURE EARNERS "I know that some people would say it's not free enterprise, but what's free enterprise when you're sitting home and you get a bill that some guy set up in an office on Park Avenue and they said, 'let's charge a fee that's too high,'" he continued. "So I'm all for that." Trump added, "The credit card companies, they're getting too much, the fees are too high and the interests are too high." The president's comments come as nationwide credit card balances have soared to a record $1.29 trillion — a 67% surge since early 2021, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Trump previously called for a one-year cap limiting credit card interest rates to 10% in a Truth Social post in January. MAMDANI THANKS TRUMP FOR HELPING SMALL BUSINESSES IN NYC, NATIONWIDE: 'PRESIDENT HAS DELIVERED RELIEF' He argued at the time that the Biden administration had allowed rates to rise as high as 20% to 30% and that Americans were being "ripped off" by credit card companies. Trump's renewed interest in the cap drew support from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, including Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., who has previously introduced legislation to cap credit card interest rates. "The President is right. Let's pass my bill to cap credit card interest fees," Hawley wrote on X. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., also welcomed Trump's remarks. TRUMP ADMIN POURING $480M LOAN INTO GULF OF AMERICA OIL AND GAS PROJECT "Let's cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money," Warren posted on X in response to Trump's interview. Major banking industry organizations have warned that imposing a 10% cap could limit access to credit, particularly for consumers with lower credit scores. In a joint statement earlier this year, several banking associations warned that the proposal could force lenders to reduce credit availability and push borrowers toward more expensive alternatives, calling the cap "devastating" for millions of Americans. CLICK HERE TO GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO Despite opposition from the banking industry, Trump's proposal could receive renewed attention when Democrats take control of Congress in January, with several lawmakers already expressing support for limiting credit card interest rates.
news.summary: Donald Trump says he would work with Democrats on a 10% credit card interest rate cap as the New York Fed reports balances have hit a record $1.29 trillion.

news.title: FBI's national crime database targeted in hack, Trump says
news.text:
President Donald Trump said in an interview Saturday that the FBI’s National Crime Information Center database was targeted in a hack.

Trump made the claim during a phone interview with Fox News.

"Well, we just heard about it, and I will say that it's not good. I don't like that," he said during the interview.

A law enforcement source confirmed to ABC News that the database was hacked.

The NCIC is a repository of criminal justice information, including data on criminal record history, current fugitives, stolen property, and missing persons, according to the FBI.

The FBI declined to comment.

The perpetrators behind the hack and the scale of the intrusion are currently unclear.

Federal, state, and local law enforcement use the database for their investigations, according to retired FBI Supervisory Special Agent Jason Pack.

"Whether you’re a deputy sheriff in rural Tennessee, a state trooper working the interstate or an FBI agent investigating a fugitive, NCIC is how you check wanted persons, stolen vehicles, missing persons and other critical information," Pack told ABC News.

"The FBI maintains the system, but it’s connected to law enforcement agencies all across the country. And that’s important when we start talking about how somebody might have gotten in," he added.

Pack said that he believed the FBI will have its best cyber investigators on the case. "Officers need to know that when they run somebody through NCIC, the information coming back is accurate," he said. "Because sometimes that information can mean the difference between an officer going home at the end of a shift or not."

During the interview, the president implied without providing evidence that the hack might include information related to the investigations into Russian interference into the 2016 election, which he has repeatedly called a "hoax," and the phone call he made to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy that led to his first impeachment by Congress.

The NCIC would not have information regarding those investigations in its database.

Russian hackers allegedly hacked Democratic National Committee emails during the summer of the 2016 campaign. 

Then presidential candidate Trump said at the time he hoped Russian hackers reportedly responsible would also find thousands of private emails deleted by former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton.

"Russia, if you're listening, I hope you're able to find the 30,000 emails that are missing," he said. Later, Trump said he was being sarcastic.

The White House hasn't immediately commented about the incident.

ABC News' Ivan Pereira contributed to this report.

Editor's note: This story has been updated.
news.summary: President Donald Trump confirmed on Saturday that the FBI’s National Crime Information Center database was targeted in a hack.
news.author: Luke Barr,Nicholas Kerr

news.title: Pentagon Imposes Limits On Military Ties With Canada Amid Strained Relations
news.text: US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has imposed new restrictions on military cooperation with Canada, according to US media, as the Pentagon said Saturday it was refocusing the relationship around American defense priorities.Hegseth issued the directive in a classified memo circulated last week, The Washington Post reported Friday, citing officials familiar with the decision.The precise scope of the restrictions was unclear, and the Post said it had not seen the memo."The Department of War is taking steps to ensure its engagements with Canada advance tangible US defense objectives and ultimately support a reinvigorated defense relationship," chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told AFP, when asked to comment on the report.He said Washington was "prioritizing opportunities for bilateral cooperation" to strengthen the defense of the Americas, "while supporting Canada's ability to meet NATO obligations."The Trump administration has devoted considerable military and diplomatic resources over the past year to fighting drug trafficking in Latin America, and has also consistently complained of NATO allies not spending enough on defense."This guidance does not impact defense intelligence cooperation, our binational NORAD command, or our cooperation through NATO," Parnell added.NORAD is the joint US-Canadian command responsible for monitoring and defending North American airspace.The reported restrictions come amid strained relations between the longtime allies under President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly suggested Canada should become the 51st US state.Trump has imposed tariffs on Canadian goods and criticized Ottawa's defense spending, while Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has firmly rejected any suggestion of annexation.Canada's Ministry of National Defence, when reached for comment on the Washington Post report, said in a statement that it "would not speculate on media reports of this nature.""Canada and the United States have a long history of defence cooperation built on a shared commitment to continental defence and protecting our collective security around the globe. This collaborative work continues," said the statement, shared by spokesman Tony Wright.(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)
news.summary: The Trump administration has devoted considerable military and diplomatic resources over the past year to fighting drug trafficking in Latin America
news.author: Agence France Presse

news.title: Mexico captures top cartel boss El Chapo Isidro, violence erupts in Sinaloa
news.text: Gunfire rang out, trucks burned and Mexican forces clashed with cartel gunmen in the state of Sinaloa overnight as Mexican authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro." Meza Flores was one of the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives. He climbed the cartel ranks to lead the Beltran Leyva cartel and later became the leader of his own group, the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. The United States had a USD 5 million reward offer for information leading to his arrest, and he was wanted for trafficking drugs to the US and illegally carrying firearms.Mexico's government said in a report early Saturday that intelligence from the Trump administration helped authorities capture him, but provided few details about how authorities in Mexico and the United States coordinated to detain Meza Flores.He was also a key ally to "Los Mayos," a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, which was designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the Trump administration last year. His capture represents a blow to the cartel as it fights with another faction for control of the northern Mexican state.Authorities in the United States and Mexico celebrated the arrest as a security win. US President Donald Trump has pressured Mexico's government to go after criminal groups.As a fierce firefight settled into a tense calm Saturday, experts warn that picking off capos could set off another wave of violence in a region already caught up in a power struggle between warring cartel factions.Mexican forces' move against cartel fuels violenceThe capture of Meza Flores and his No. 2 in the city of Guasave, Sinaloa, set off a wave of violence when a firefight broke out around 7 pm on Friday according to residents of the 290,000-person municipality. Soon, military helicopters and drones were flying overhead and opened fire on key locations across the city.Videos show screaming civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, burning cars and businesses, and circling helicopters shooting at people below. Such shows of force by cartels are common following the capture or killing of leaders."The fighting was happening all over Guasave," said Alma Camacho, a Guasave resident and local journalist. "It spread throughout the city." Mexican authorities said that they used "stealth and surprise" to arrest Meza Flores, establishing a security perimeter around the building where he was located. After coming under attack with guns and explosives from suspected cartel operatives, armed forces personnel entered a home and detained him. He was later taken by aircraft to Mexico City to appear before prosecutors.Video shared by authorities shows heavily armed men in camouflage escorting a man through a dimly lit house and putting him in the back of a truck. No casualties have been reported so far as a result of the operation.Because of the violence, the Mexican army and National Guard special forces were unable to extract Meza Flores from Guasave until 4 a.m. on Saturday, said a federal official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to discuss the case."Getting him (Meza Flores) out was extraordinary," the official said, describing an intense response by members of the criminal group who maintained at least "10 roadblocks" with burning vehicles on Guasave's streets.Terror in SinaloaGuasave resident and firefighter Paola Sanchez said that thousands of people were terrorized late Friday as they took shelter from intense gunfire in grocery stores and other locations."Last night, many businesses were burned ... along with cars and trucks," Sanchez told The Associated Press.She said that the city's firefighters had to take shelter at their station and wait until Saturday morning for orders from their superiors to dispatch the first crews to check whether any businesses or vehicles were still burning.An uneasy calm seemed to settle over the city Saturday. Mexican Security Secretary Omar Garcia Harfuch wrote on X on Saturday morning that armed forces would remain deployed in Sinaloa state to protect civilians. Authorities didn't provide details on how many people were wounded or killed in the clashes.Burned out trucks continued to line the freeway leading into the town, blocking roadways on Saturday."The aftermath of last night's war still lingers. Burned cars in the streets, several Oxxo stores completely burned down," Camacho said, referring to a chain of convenience stores in Mexico.Guasave residents remained "very afraid" because security forces were absent from the streets, Camacho said.Capture prompts celebration and warningsMeza Flores' detention marks another high-profile capture of a cartel leader as Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum faces pressure from Trump to crack down on cartels. Sheinbaum has gone after illegal groups more aggressively than her predecessors, and homicides have dipped significantly in her two years in office.The US and Mexican governments celebrated the capture on Saturday, with the DEA commending Mexican authorities."Results like these don't happen overnight. They are built on sustained cooperation and trust. This is what partners can accomplish together," US Ambassador Ronald Johnson said in an X post. "We will continue the hunt." Mexican Security Secretary Garcia Harfuch called the detention "an important step in pacifying Sinaloa." Sheinbaum's government has targeted a number of cartel kingpins, including Jalisco New Generation Cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as " El Mencho," who was killed by the military in February.Mexican security analyst David Saucedo said that the capture of Meza Flores marked another case of the governments of Mexico and the US increasingly falling back on a longstanding security strategy that critics warn could fuel more violence in the long run.The so-called kingpin strategy relies on zeroing in on capos like Meza Flores as a way to combat cartels. But experts say that it often triggers violent power disputes among groups, like the one underway in Sinaloa."What is evident is this is a product of pressure from the United States," Saucedo said. "What they do is capture high-profile kingpins - the leaders - but they don't dismantle the entire organization. They arrested the No. 1 and No. 2, but the entire network of hit men, street-level drug dealers, businesses and political and police connections remains intact.
news.summary:
Gunfire rang out, trucks burned and Mexican forces clashed with cartel gunmen in the state of Sinaloa overnight as Mexican authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro."
Meza Flores was one of the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives. He climbed the cartel ranks to lead the Beltran Leyva cartel and later became the leader of his own group, the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. The United States had a USD 5 million reward offer for information leading to his arrest, and he was wanted for trafficking drugs to the US and illegally carrying firearms.
Mexico's government said in a report early Saturday that intelligence from the Trump administration helped authorities capture him, but provided few details about how authorities in Mexico and the United States coordinated to detain Meza Flores.

news.title: Trump vows to work with Democrats to cap credit card interest rates at 10%
news.text:
PTITrump is seeking bipartisan support to cap credit card interest rates at 10%, reviving a campaign pledge as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress amid record US credit card debt.

New York: President Donald Trump said Saturday that he would work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates, hoping to fulfill a promise he made on the 2024 campaign trail but couldn't deliver on because of industry pressure and a lack of interest from his fellow Republicans."I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot," Trump told Fox News Channel's "Saturday in America."Democrats and the Republican president have both backed capping credit card interest rates, with the standard proposal being capping rates at 10%. It would substantially reduce what credit card companies can charge customers. The median credit card interest rate is roughly 22.2%, according to an August survey by the New York Federal Reserve.Trump proposed capping credit card interest rates in January, as part of the White House's affordability push. Banks and credit card companies immediately and aggressively opposed the proposal, saying any interest rate cap would force them to cancel cards for the poor and less creditworthy customers or substantially cut back on the rewards they offer when customers spend on their cards.The proposal also did not sit well with Republicans, and there was little effort by the GOP-controlled Congress to fulfill Trump's promise.Live EventsThat could change now that Democrats will control both the House and Senate. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who is expected to be the next chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has said repeatedly she wants to cap rates.In response to the Fox News interview, Warren said: "Let's cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money."Other Democrats have endorsed the idea in various ways, including Rep. Maxine Waters of California, a powerful Democrat who sits on the House Financial Services Committee. Among Republicans, Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri has proposed several caps on credit card interest rates, as recently as this year when Trump made his proposal."Congress should pass my bipartisan bill to cap these rates and deliver relief right away," Hawley said at the time.Researchers who studied Trump's campaign pledge after it was first announced found that Americans would save roughly $100 billion in interest a year if credit card rates were capped at 10%. The same researchers found that while the credit card industry would take a major hit, it would still be profitable, although credit card rewards and other perks might be scaled back.About 195 million people in the United States had credit cards in 2024 and were assessed $160 billion in interest charges, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says.Americans are now carrying more credit card debt than ever, to the tune of about $1.23 trillion, according to figures from the New York Federal Reserve for the third quarter last year.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Trump Says Iran Deal Would Be Permanent
news.text: Washington DC: US President Donald Trump on Saturday said that any potential agreement with Iran would be "permanent" and aimed at preventing Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons, reiterating his insistence on securing what he described as a genuine and lasting deal with the country."I'm going to make a deal that is going to be permanent. I’m not going to let somebody allow them to have a nuclear weapon," Trump said, expressing his determination to ensure that Iran does not develop nuclear weapons.In an interview with Fox News, Trump also said he had never been particularly interested in regime change in Iran while describing his attacks on the country's senior leadership as a significant shift for the Iranian regime. He characterised Iran's new leadership as "more rational", but questioned its reliability in negotiations, alleging that Tehran had a history of making agreements and subsequently breaking them.The latest remarks come amid continuing tensions between Washington and Tehran, with Trump repeatedly expressing dissatisfaction over the terms Iran has been willing to offer in negotiations.Earlier on Friday, following his visit to China, Trump launched a sharp criticism of Tehran, accusing Iran of misleading people for decades and insisting that any agreement with Washington must meet US expectations.Speaking at a press conference, the US President linked fluctuations in gasoline prices to the outcome of negotiations with Iran, arguing that Tehran wanted an agreement but had not offered terms acceptable to him."The prices of gasoline now, that also depends on how we settle up with Iran.
