It's 51 years," Trump said.Taking a further swipe at Tehran, Trump accused Iran of misleading people over the past five decades, remarking, "They've been bullsh***ing people for 51 years."Trump's latest comments underscore his continued push for an agreement that would prevent Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons, while maintaining that Washington would not accept a deal that falls short of its expectations.His remarks come amid continuing tensions in West Asia, with Washington weighing its options regarding Iran, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has reportedly urged the US administration to consider renewed military action against Tehran.While Trump has indicated that he is seeking a lasting diplomatic agreement, his statements also reflect his continued criticism of Iran's negotiating approach and the terms offered by Tehran.

news.title: ICE detains 2 Alaska Airlines passengers at Seattle airport
news.text:
Masked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers detained two passengers Saturday on a crowded jet bridge at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as travelers boarded a Los Angeles-bound flight, the Port of Seattle said.

The arrests delayed Alaska Airlines Flight 1306, scheduled to depart at 8:10 a.m., until 11:03 a.m. The disruption came during a busy travel weekend before Thanksgiving.

ICE said the operation targeted Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza for arrest. The Department of Homeland Security described him to Newsweek as "an illegal alien from Mexico who overstayed his visa in violation of our nation's laws."

The agency said another passenger, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, "hurled hot coffee on the officers" and was arrested. ICE said Hernandez Mejia, like Mendoza, is Mexican and remained in the U.S. beyond her visa's expiration.

She could face a charge of assaulting a federal officer, The Associated Press reported, while DHS told Newsweek she will be charged.

DHS also said "other travelers began to obstruct and assault our law enforcement officers—a federal crime and a felony."

Footage described by The Seattle Times showed masked men tying a woman's hands near the aircraft cabin. Someone else who appeared to step in was thrown to the ground.

A witness told The Seattle Times that agents pulled a traveler through a side door, were locked outside and motioned to an airline worker to reopen it. "An Alaska agent let them back in, and they said to (another) woman that she threw coffee on them and that's a federal crime against an agent," the witness told The Seattle Times.

CBS News reported that video showed officers dragging away at least one person while a woman screamed that her daughter was being taken and had a work permit. Newsweek quoted the woman as saying, "They're taking my dad."

Someone familiar with the case told KING 5 that, to that person's understanding, the two detainees came to the U.S. legally and are going through the immigration process.

It was not immediately known where the two were being held, if either had legal representation or if Hernandez Mejia had been charged.

ICE has increased airport arrests since the summer, particularly of people who overstayed visas. The Deportation Data Project found 568 airport-linked ICE arrests in government records from Jan. 20, 2025, to March 10, 2026, compared with 108 during the same period before President Donald Trump's second administration.

Alaska Airlines said "the law enforcement activity was not previously known to us," though Newsweek reported that the carrier said it had received prior notification. "We recognize how distressing this incident has been for affected employees and guests," the airline said. Alaska said it is working with the Port of Seattle, the airport's manager, to determine whether protocols were followed.

The Port said it was "outraged" and that airport immigration enforcement takes place without its participation or knowledge. Local federal immigration authorities had previously agreed to airport protocols, the Port said, and it is discussing with DHS whether any were breached.

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, wrote on X that ICE is "completely and totally out of control" and that he is "outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways." In the videos, one agent identifies himself as a federal officer.

ICE is completely and totally out of control. Like many Americans, I’m outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities. Today’s actions at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport are— Governor Bob Ferguson (@GovBobFerguson) November 21, 2026

"The video is horrific and it is chilling," Ferguson said at a news conference Saturday, where he called for ICE's abolition. He said he believes the officers broke a state law he signed in March that limits facial coverings for law enforcement officers.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal said earlier this month that she plans oversight hearings as she prepares to lead a House Judiciary subcommittee. Sen. Patty Murray wrote on X that she was demanding answers from DHS and that Trump "answers to a Democratic Congress on January 3rd."
news.summary: The Port of Seattle said it was outraged and is discussing with federal officials whether airport protocols were breached.

news.title: Trump claims recent FBI hack could have positive impact and help uncover truth about 'hoaxes'
news.text:
President Donald Trump has offered an unexpected silver lining to reports of a cyberattack targeting the FBI—suggesting the breach could end up revealing information about past political "hoaxes" and "voter fraud."

Calling in live to Fox News’ Saturday in America with host Kayleigh McEnany on Saturday, November 21, the 80-year-old president was asked for his reaction to reports that hackers had breached an FBI criminal database earlier in the week.

“Well, we just heard about it, and I will say that it’s not good, I don’t like that, but maybe we'll learn things we would've never learned otherwise,” Trump said during the phone interview. “You had the Russia Russia Russia hoax. We call it Ukraine. The Ukraine Ukraine Ukraine hoax. The perfect phone call. Maybe we'll learn about them. Maybe we'll learn about all the voter fraud that took place. So I always like to put things on a positive spin.” 

Trump went on to question who might be behind the intrusion, adding that he believed the public "should hear about" details surrounding the 2016 Russia investigation because "it actually put our country in danger." 

Second FBI Breach in Recent Months

According to reports, the cyberattack occurred on Thursday, November 19, targeting the National Crime Information Center (NCIC)—a vital electronic database connecting federal, state, and local police departments nationwide to share records on fugitives, missing persons, outstanding warrants, and criminal background checks. 

Two sources familiar with the investigation told CNN that the incident marks the second reported breach involving the bureau in recent months, following a September cyberattack attributed to the ShinyHunters hacking group that targeted an FBI recruitment portal. Officials have not yet publicly confirmed the identity of the latest attackers or whether sensitive law enforcement records were copied or altered. 

Following the initial reports, FBI Director Kash Patel appeared on Fox News to defend the agency’s cybersecurity posture, pointing to an operation completed months earlier urging private companies to patch system vulnerabilities.

Broader Wave of Federal Cyber Concerns

News of the FBI intrusion coincided with a separate cybersecurity breach at the U.S. Department of Agriculture. 

USDA employees were notified on Thursday that a system used to facilitate payments to farmers had been compromised, with officials warning that the breach could potentially give attackers a backdoor to more sensitive agency material. 

The back-to-back incidents come as the Trump administration faces mounting scrutiny over a string of recent technical outages affecting major U.S. institutions—including banks, the National Security Agency, and the Federal Aviation Administration’s air traffic control network—amid ongoing concerns over potential cyberattacks.
news.summary: The President tried to put a positive spin on the security breach that saw hackers access the governmental crime database

news.title: Trump Posts Senator-Elect El-Sayed's Gold 'TrumpCare' Card Without Comment
news.text:
President Donald Trump on Saturday reposted Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed’s (D-MI) pitch for a government-run health care program branded “TrumpCare,” adding no comment of his own.

The president shared the message on his Truth Social account Saturday afternoon with no caption attached. El-Sayed told FOX 2 Detroit he was ready to move on it.

“President Trump, give me a call. I’m happy to chat,” the Michigan Democrat said.

El-Sayed’s mock-up is a gold insurance card stamped with Trump’s name and signature. Show it at any doctor, hospital, clinic, or pharmacy in the country, the back says. Newsweek reported the look borrows from the Trump Gold Card, the administration’s $1 million residency program for wealthy foreigners.

That post went up Nov. 12 and has drawn more than 11 million views. “Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave,” El-Sayed wrote. The senator-elect has argued that a single government payer would equalize reimbursement rates he claims leave black and Arab patients with worse treatment.

Trump spent part of Saturday talking up a deal with the incoming Democrat majorities.

“There’s a chance we could get great healthcare and a lot of other things, and we can do it in a bipartisan way,” he told Fox News host Kayleigh McEnany on “Saturday in America. The president also said he was prepared to reject whatever Democrats send him. “I could sit there for two years and one month and just veto everything,” he said.

His own White House answered the same pitch four days earlier. Spokeswoman Allison Schuster told Fox News Digital the proposal “should really be called ‘Medicare for None'” because it “destroys access to the life-saving care Americans rely on daily.” The administration cited the Council of Economic Advisers. Its analysts put the added deficit at roughly $47.4 trillion from 2027 to 2036 if no new taxes are raised.

El-Sayed had a different message for Trump two weeks ago. On ABC’s This Week, the first Muslim elected to the Senate called the president an “unserious fool” and faulted him over the Iran war, tariffs on Canada, and cuts to Medicaid.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) became speaker-designate this past week in a caucus vote in which 11 Democrats opposed him. El-Sayed takes the oath in January.

President Donald Trump on Saturday reposted Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed's (D-MI) pitch for a government-run health care program branded "TrumpCare," adding no comment of his own.

news.title: Ultimate guide to getting cheaper heating oil: Why timing is everything, the little-known sites that leak the best prices and how joining forces with neighbours can unlock deals
news.text:
Households that are reliant on oil for heating have seen the cost more than double this year – and they could be forced to fork out hundreds extra during cold snaps this winter.

Some 1.5 million households use oil for central heating while a further 200,000 homes use liquefied petroleum gas (LPG).

The cost of filling a 1,000-litre tank of oil has leapt from about £600 in early February to £1,200 this month as a result of the soaring international prices.

This was triggered by the attack on Iran by the US in February, after which the flow of oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz was cut off. This crucial passage in the Middle East was used to transport a fifth of the world’s oil supplies.

The price of crude oil jumped from about $65 a barrel when the war began to as high as $115 last month. It still stood at more than $90 last week.

Unlike with electricity and domestic gas from the National Grid, heating oil and LPG have not been capped by the energy watchdog Ofgem, leaving households that rely on it the worst hit.

Last month, Chancellor John Healey announced that a 4 per cent import duty on this oil would be suspended from November 26 until the end of 2028. But campaign groups have warned this will not be enough.

Industry experts say any savings made on the import duty will be gobbled up by suppliers, leaving households just a few pounds better off.

But if you are prepared to take matters into your own hands, there are ways of unlocking cheaper heating oil. Here’s why timing is everything and how your neighbours may be the key to saving money.

Cost of waiting

The relief on import duty will come into effect on Thursday, but it is unlikely to offer the respite households had been hoping for.

Simon Francis, co-ordinator for action group End Fuel Poverty Coalition, says: ‘Homes have seen the price of their fuel rocket by hundreds of pounds in the past year and will not be impressed by these unregulated cuts that are not a cap.

‘Even if suppliers pass on savings, it will cut bills by only a few pounds – just a drop in the oil tank.’

A spokesman for East Sussex-based fuel provider Rye Oil says: ‘Are you going to feel the benefit of the duty drop? The 4 per cent decrease is more than likely to become a profit gain for the export/import company.’ It adds: ‘The 4 per cent on a kerosene price of £1.16 per litre equates to about 4.4p per litre. On the industry standard minimum order of 500 litres this would be £23. A nice saving if it all passes downstream.’

The policy may knock a few pounds off bills but customers should be wary of waiting too long before putting in an order for heating oil. As the weather turns colder, demand will rise.

All about timing

The key is in timing a purchase, not least in a climate where prices can swing so dramatically.

Cara Martin, 43, from North Wales, who relies on heating oil to warm her three-bedroom semi-detached Victorian house, discovered firsthand just how much of a difference lucky timing can make.

She ordered a full tank of oil in July, when prices were far lower, and is now able to keep her home in Gwynedd warm and toasty throughout winter.

Cara says: ‘My stroke of luck was not to trust everything Donald Trump says. I had a feeling, when a ceasefire was announced in summer and prices dropped to near pre-war levels, that it would not last.

‘I put in an order when no one else was thinking of heating the home but wondering how to pay for their summer holidays. Just 24 hours later, costs rocketed.’

Cara, a publisher who co-wrote the book Backgarden Chickens And Other Poultry with her father John Harrison, paid £600 for a 1,000-litre tank of oil. Had she waited until this month to order, she could have paid twice as much.

It means the writer is now one of a minority who can afford to heat the home she shares with husband Gary, also 43, and their son Gabriel, 13. They will be safe from the freezing temperatures of minus 10C that will sweep off Snowdonia towards her home this winter, though Cara’s chickens may struggle.

However, she fears the winter will get only tougher, saying: ‘Waiting for prices to fall might be a fool’s game. When it gets colder, demand rises along with prices. You could be worse off.’

Finding the best price

Comparison websites – such as Boiler Juice, HomeFuels Direct and Fueltool – can provide the best oil price deals for where you live.

If you have a local supplier who you trust, contact them and ask if they can beat the best price from these comparison websites.

Cara says: ‘It’s best if you support your local supplier and they know the area well. Asking them to match a better price is not cheeky but sound business decisions.’

Tariffs are lower for those willing to wait at least a week for their order to arrive – you may pay up to 10 per cent more for an emergency next-day delivery. For those who can afford to buy in bulk, ordering at least 1,000 litres rather than 500 litres can knock a couple of pence per litre off the bill. This can provide a £20 saving.

To make the most of the savings by having increased purchasing power, it is also worth joining – or even forming – a club with neighbours. Websites such as The Oil-Club provide details of groups in your area. They are made up of households that have joined forces for a bulk order.

It costs nothing to sign up and deliveries are typically scheduled for a given period, where you can fill up as much as you need.

Those that require emergency deliveries will have to pay extra. This can be as much as 13p a litre extra – so a 1,000-litre tank could cost £130 more to fill if you want the fuel the next day rather than on a scheduled visit.

Francis says: ‘Communities that rely on oil have to look after each other – and you should check on vulnerable neighbours as many suffer in silence.

‘By working together, you can save money.’

You might pay 5 per cent less as a club member, according to The Oil-Club. This could knock £60 off a 1,000 litre fill up that previously cost £1,200.

A typical home might get through 2,000 litres of oil a year – so you can save more than £100 a year as a member.

Steps to help

The most cost-effective measure you can take is making sure your home is properly insulated.

As much as £500 a year of heating is wasted due to poor insulation, with a third escaping out the roof and a third through walls.

Visit the Energy Saving Trust website for guidance.

You might also look at alternative heating sources. The Government is encouraging households to install air source heat pumps as part of its Net Zero aim for greenhouse gas emissions by 2050.

For homes willing to replace an oil or LPG system, there is an offer of a £9,000 grant – £1,500 more than otherwise – available until March. However, it typically costs £15,000 to get one installed.

James Stalker, owner of heating company Eco Pro Renewables in Devon, says: ‘Your installer applies for the grant and takes it off the quote, so you never wait to claim it back. Ask any installer for a running-cost estimate based on a heat-loss survey of your home.’

And while it might seem an unnecessary expense, the cost of servicing your boiler every year – usually about £100 – can pay for itself as the heating system will run more efficiently.

A £1 billion government-backed Crisis and Resilience Fund was set up in April this year to offer financial help to low-income families facing a crisis due to high energy bills. Contact your local council via its website to ask if you are eligible for help. Details can also be found via the Government website gov.uk.

You need not receive benefits to qualify but must be vulnerable and show you struggle to buy essentials. The amount you get depends on your council, but in some areas it is a one-off payment of up to £250.
news.summary: Households that are reliant on oil for heating have seen the cost more than double this year. But if you are prepared to take matters into your own hands, there are ways of unlocking cheaper oil.

news.title: Democrats who swept into the Senate promised change. A leadership vote is testing them early
news.text:
APDemocrats' incoming senators are weighing whether to retain Chuck Schumer or back Chris Van Hollen in a leadership contest that is testing the party's promise of generational change.

Washington: The Democratic Party's incoming senators haven't even been sworn into office yet, but the decision over who will lead their new majority is already testing the promise of change they made as candidates.The 13 new Democrats are part of the largest incoming Senate class in decades, with several winning in Republican strongholds by promising to shake up Washington and be independent voices. Now they are caught up in a classic insider fight, forced to decide whether to stick with longtime Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York or back challenger Chris Van Hollen of Maryland.Newly elected progressives, including Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, have backed Van Hollen, who is taking on Schumer with promises of a more aggressive legislative approach. Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown of Ohio, who is returning to Washington after losing his seat in 2024, supports Schumer.But the incoming senators from traditionally Republican states such as Texas, Mississippi, Iowa and South Carolina, whose victories helped deliver Democrats the majority, have so far largely avoided taking sides publicly. Annie Andrews of South Carolina has said she is talking with both candidates. Scott Colom of Mississippi says he wants to get to know them better before deciding and describes himself as being in "listening mode."Kansas Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton said Thursday he would not back Schumer, but declined to endorse anyone.Live Events"I'm looking for someone who is going to bring people together," Hamilton told MSNow. "Right now, in places like Kansas, there's a lot of people who don't feel that in Chuck Schumer."Schumer's long-standing relationships and knowledge of Senate machinery are a big advantage heading into the Dec. 1 vote, which will be held by secret ballot. He also oversees Senate Democrats' campaign spending group, funneling millions into many of the races and, in some cases, recruiting the candidates to run in the first place.But the reluctance of many incoming senators to commit has put an unusual spotlight on first-term lawmakers who could help shape the party's direction in the new Congress."We should be very embracing of the new people who have been through fire to get here," said Hawaii Sen. Mazie Hirono, who is supporting Schumer. "We have to make sure that all these voices are heard, and they've got a lot of talent to bring to the table."The senators who campaigned for changeMany of the incoming senators campaigned as political outsiders, promising to bring fresh perspectives to a Washington establishment they argued had failed ordinary Americans.Andrews, a 46-year-old pediatrician, became the first Democrat in nearly three decades to win a Senate race in South Carolina. She called for "generational change" and said that she would not support Schumer.But she has also rejected policies that Van Hollen supports, such as "Medicare for All." On a press call Tuesday, Andrews said she has made "no decision" on the majority leader's race."The way I assess the situation as it is right now is that the generational change is represented by this incredibly dynamic incoming freshman class of senators," Andrews said.Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico called for "new blood" in the Democratic Party, arguing that fresh perspectives were needed to change a political system that had failed. But Talarico has stopped short of rejecting Schumer, saying in a CBS interview two days after the Nov. 3 election that he would meet with the leadership candidates and ask "tough questions."Iowa Sen.-elect Josh Turek has taken a similar approach, saying his decision will depend on which candidate best reflects the priorities he campaigned on. During a news conference Monday, he said that he had met with Schumer and Van Hollen and was waiting for "further updates" on questions he had."Whoever provides those answers to me that most closely align with my common sense, prairie populist agenda that I've been running on for the last year and a half, that's who I'll support," Turek said.Alaska Sen.-elect Mary Peltola, whose race was officially called on Wednesday, told The Associated Press soon after that she had not yet thought about the leadership race.El-Sayed and Flanagan have been among the staunch supporters of Van Hollen. Another progressive, Maine Sen.-elect Troy Jackson, has said he wouldn't support Schumer but hasn't yet said he would vote for Van Hollen.Schumer backed alternative candidates during the primaries in all three races. He supported all three once they were nominated.A private decision has become a public fightSenate leadership elections have traditionally been private affairs, decided by lawmakers in closed-door, secret-ballot votes that are shaped by the complicated inner workings of the Senate. The job requires holding together a caucus with competing political interests, a responsibility that doesn't always align with the demands of the party's most vocal activists.Schumer's allies point to his success in doing that job, most recently in the midterms. He helped recruit candidates such as Brown, Peltola and North Carolina Sen.-elect Roy Cooper, while his allied super PAC was the largest Democratic spender in tightly contested races such as in Michigan and Maine."When the manager takes you to the World Series, you give him another contract," Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego said.But Democrats are also facing pressure from some in their base to confront Republican President Donald Trump more aggressively while delivering on ambitious policy promises. Large progressive organizations, including MoveOn and Indivisible, have endorsed Van Hollen, while many senators' offices have been flooded with calls urging them to reject Schumer."Our members are tired of politicians content with incrementalism - they want bold, creative leadership that will help Democrats usher in affordability and accountability without delay or compromise in the next Congress," MoveOn's executive director, Joel Payne, said in a statement.At a Schumer news conference Wednesday, several activists shouted from a distance, "Step down, Schumer! Step down, Schumer!"The fifth-term senator has not said whether his term ending in 2028 will be his last.Van Hollen, a supporter of progressive priorities including Medicare for All and restrictions on offensive weapons transfers to Israel, has promised a more confrontational approach to Trump, an ambitious economic agenda and changes to how the party operates in primaries.The calls for change extend beyond the first-term lawmakersThe leadership fight has also drawn in more established Democrats, including senators whose political ambitions may include higher office.Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, fresh off a reelection victory in a presidential battleground state, is among the Democrats whose names have surfaced as potential White House contenders in 2028. Ossoff has served under Schumer's leadership for nearly six years."I haven't committed to any candidate, and I'll hear everybody out," Ossoff said this week.Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, elected in 2024 and now contemplating a presidential bid, said Thursday she was supporting Van Hollen. A moderate who has called for change in Senate leadership, Slotkin has also been critical of some of Van Hollen's more progressive policies, underscoring how the leadership fight cuts across the party's ideological divisions."Because I've been clear that I wasn't supporting Schumer, I will be supporting Chris Van Hollen," Slotkin said.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Jeffry Sachs explained logic of Donald Trump’s statements on Taiwan in Shenzhen
news.text:
MOSCOW, November 22. /TASS/. US economist and Director of the Center for Sustainable Development at Columbia University Jeffrey Sachs explained the logic of statements made by the US President Donald Trump on the issue of Taiwan at the APEC summit in Shenzhen.

"The basis for a durable relationship is again the principle of spheres of security. For the United States, that means ending the containment policy toward China, honoring the One China policy that every US administration has affirmed since 1972, and ending the American arming of Taiwan," Sachs told TASS in an interview in conclusion of the APEC summit.

For the United States and China, "it means cooperating on challenges that no country can address alone, including climate change, pandemic preparedness, the governance of artificial intelligence, and the stability of the world economy," he noted.

"The limits lie mainly in Washington, where a bipartisan anti-China sentiment remains strong in Congress and in the security establishment, based on prejudices rather than realism," the economist said.

Despite presence of barriers in developing relations between Washington and Beijing, "the logic of cooperation is also powerful, and the American business community understands well that the US economy benefits importantly from two-way trade with China," he added.
news.summary: The basis for a durable relationship is again the principle of spheres of security, and for the United States, that means ending the containment policy toward China, Director of the Center for Sustainable Development at Columbia University said
news.author: Tass

news.title: Canada defense chief sees no change despite reported US military curbs
news.text:
HALIFAX, Nova Scotia: Canadian Defense Minister David McGuinty said on Saturday he had seen no change in military cooperation with the United States, despite a reported Pentagon directive imposing new restrictions on defense ties between the longtime allies.

McGuinty said he had not seen a classified memo that US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth reportedly circulated last week setting out constraints on military cooperation with Canada.

“I still see no daylight between what we’re doing, military to military, and otherwise,” McGuinty told Reuters on the sidelines of a security conference in Halifax.

He said the two countries’ armed forces continued working “hand in glove” on operations, including efforts to stop trafficking of cocaine, fentanyl and other illegal drugs in the Caribbean, integrated missile systems and scrambling fighter jets to respond to threats across North America.

The Washington Post reported Friday that Hegseth had issued the classified directive, citing officials familiar with the decision. The precise scope of the reported restrictions remained unclear, and the newspaper said it had not seen the memo.

The Pentagon said it was refocusing its relationship with Canada around US defense priorities.

“The Department of War is taking steps to ensure its engagements with Canada advance tangible US defense objectives and ultimately support a reinvigorated defense relationship,” chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told AFP.

Washington was prioritizing bilateral cooperation to strengthen the defense of the Americas while supporting Canada's ability to meet its NATO commitments, Parnell said.

He said the guidance did not affect defense intelligence cooperation, the binational North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) or cooperation through NATO.

US Senator Mike Rounds, a South Dakota Republican, said defense officials had briefed him on the memo, which he described as containing no major new measures beyond steps American military officials had taken for years.

Canada's Defense Ministry said it would not speculate on media reports but stressed that defense cooperation between the two countries continued.

“Canada and the United States have a long history of defense cooperation built on a shared commitment to continental defense and protecting our collective security around the globe. This collaborative work continues,” spokesman Tony Wright said in a statement.

McGuinty said the countries' 70-year partnership under NORAD had provided an effective continental defense system and that Ottawa wanted to continue investing in and cooperating through it.

The reported Pentagon move comes amid strained relations under US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly suggested Canada should become the 51st US state, imposed tariffs on Canadian goods and criticized Ottawa's defense spending.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has rejected Trump's annexation rhetoric and called for a reassessment of the global security order, prompting Ottawa to accelerate its defense investments.

McGuinty said Canada needed to take greater responsibility for its own security, particularly in the Arctic, and was working to develop a domestic alternative to Starlink satellite communications to safeguard its sovereignty.

Canada said last year it had reached NATO's defense spending target of 2 percent of gross domestic product for the first time. The government plans to increase spending to 5 percent of GDP by 2035.

“We’ve been in a comfortable position for decades, but things have now changed,” McGuinty said.
news.summary: Despite a reported Pentagon directive introducing new restrictions on military cooperation, Canadian Defense Minister David McGuinty emphasized that there has been no change in the collaboration between Canada and the United States. He stated that both nations continue to work closely on various military operations and that their defense relationship remains strong, with ongoing commitments to joint security initiatives until specific details of the reported directives are clarified.
news.author: Reuters / Afp

news.title: Deadly Sinaloa violence leaves 11 dead after capture of Mexico cartel boss El Chapo Isidro
news.text:
APThe capture of cartel boss El Chapo Isidro in a US-assisted operation triggered deadly clashes in Mexico's Sinaloa state, killing 11 people and raising fears of renewed cartel violence. (File photo)

Guasave: A burst of violence in Mexico's Sinaloa state after authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro," left at least 11 people dead, authorities said Saturday.Meza Flores, one of the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives, was captured and flown to Mexico City on Saturday after an intense firefight between Mexican forces and cartel gunmen overnight left residents of the city of Guasave terrorized and trucks and businesses burning.Mexico's Defense Ministry on Saturday afternoon said that seven alleged cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers were killed.The capo climbed the cartel ranks to lead the Beltran Leyva cartel and later became the leader of his own group, the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. The United States had a $5 million reward offer for information leading to his arrest, and he was wanted for trafficking drugs to the U.S. and illegally carrying firearms.Mexico's government said in a report early Saturday that intelligence from the Trump administration helped authorities capture him, but provided few details about how authorities in Mexico and the United States coordinated to detain Meza Flores.Live EventsHe was also a key ally to "Los Mayos," a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, which was designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the Trump administration last year. His capture represents a blow to the cartel as it fights with another faction for control of the northern Mexican state.Authorities in the United States and Mexico celebrated the arrest as a security win. U.S. President Donald Trump has pressured Mexico's government to go after criminal groups.As a fierce firefight settled into a tense calm Saturday, experts warned that picking off capos could set off another wave of violence in a region already caught up in a power struggle between warring cartel factions.Mexican forces' move against cartel fuels violenceThe capture of Meza Flores and his No. 2 in the city of Guasave, Sinaloa, set off a wave of violence when a firefight broke out around 7 p.m. on Friday, according to residents of the 290,000-person municipality. Soon, military helicopters and drones were flying overhead, and helicopters opened fire on key locations across the city.Videos show screaming civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, burning cars and businesses, and circling helicopters shooting at people below. Such shows of force by cartels are common following the capture or killing of leaders."The fighting was happening all over Guasave," said Alma Camacho, a Guasave resident and local journalist. "It spread throughout the city."Mexican authorities said that they used "stealth and surprise" to arrest Meza Flores, establishing a security perimeter around the building where he was located. After coming under attack with guns and explosives from suspected cartel operatives, armed forces personnel entered a home and detained him.Video shared by Mexico's Defense Ministry shows Meza Flores and two others being marched by heavily armed soldiers onto a military aircraft to appear before prosecutors in Mexico City. A total of eight people were detained, according to authorities.Because of the violence, the Mexican army and National Guard special forces were unable to extract Meza Flores from Guasave until 4 a.m. on Saturday, said a federal official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to discuss the case."Getting him (Meza Flores) out was extraordinary," the official said, describing an intense response by members of the criminal group who maintained at least "10 roadblocks" with burning vehicles on Guasave's streets.Terror in SinaloaGuasave resident and firefighter Paola Sanchez said that thousands of people were terrorized late Friday as they took shelter from intense gunfire in grocery stores and other locations."Last night, many businesses were burned ... along with cars and trucks," Sanchez told The Associated Press.She said that the city's firefighters had to take shelter at their station and wait until Saturday morning for orders from their superiors to dispatch the first crews to check whether any businesses or vehicles were still burning.An uneasy calm seemed to settle over the city Saturday. Mexican Security Secretary Omar Garcia Harfuch wrote on X on Saturday morning that armed forces would remain deployed in Sinaloa state to protect civilians. He lamented the deaths of the four soldiers killed in the operation.Burned-out trucks continued to line the freeway leading into the town, blocking roadways on Saturday."The aftermath of last night's war still lingers. Burned cars in the streets, several Oxxo stores completely burned down," Camacho said, referring to a chain of convenience stores in Mexico.Guasave residents remained "very afraid" because security forces were absent from the streets, Camacho said.Capture prompts celebration and warningsMeza Flores' detention marks another high-profile capture of a cartel leader as Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum faces pressure from Trump to crack down on cartels. Sheinbaum has gone after illegal groups more aggressively than her predecessors, and homicides have dipped significantly in her two years in office.The U.S. and Mexican governments celebrated the capture on Saturday, with the DEA commending Mexican authorities."Results like these don't happen overnight. They are built on sustained cooperation and trust. This is what partners can accomplish together," U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson said in an X post. "We will continue the hunt."Mexican Security Secretary Garcia Harfuch called the detention "an important step in pacifying Sinaloa."Sheinbaum's government has targeted a number of cartel kingpins, including Jalisco New Generation Cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as " El Mencho," who was killed by the military in February.Mexican security analyst David Saucedo said that the capture of Meza Flores marked another case of the governments of Mexico and the U.S. increasingly falling back on a longstanding security strategy that critics warn could fuel more violence in the long run.The so-called kingpin strategy relies on zeroing in on capos like Meza Flores as a way to combat cartels. But experts say that it often triggers violent power disputes among groups, like the one underway in Sinaloa."What is evident is this is a product of pressure from the United States," Saucedo said. "What they do is capture high-profile kingpins - the leaders - but they don't dismantle the entire organization. They arrested the No. 1 and No. 2, but the entire network of hit men, street-level drug dealers, businesses and political and police connections remains intact."Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Trump orders federal contractors to check with White House before responding to Congress
news.text:
PTITrump has tightened White House control over congressional oversight by directing federal contractors to seek administration approval before responding to lawmakers, threatening their government contracts for non-compliance.

New York: President Donald Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged, according to a new executive order.The companies must also coordinate with the White House and U.S. agencies on "appropriate responses" to any such requests, the order issued late Friday says. If they fail to comply, the White House warns their contracts could be terminated and their future work with the federal government suspended.The order is the Republican administration's latest effort to resist what are expected to be wide-ranging and aggressive oversight efforts from Democrats when they take over Congress in January. Democrats have made government contracts one of their top investigative targets, noting that federal money has been flowing to companies linked with Trump's family, particularly at the Pentagon.White House officials have already begun taking steps to exert more control over how agencies and officials respond to congressional requests, anticipating there will be a flood of investigations initiated by Democrats.Trump's counsel, Will Scharf, told federal agencies on Monday that they must seek approval from his office and the White House's Office of Legislative Affairs before agreeing to appear before Congress. Scharf also suggested in a recent letter to Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, that some congressional investigations may amount to "blatant criminality."Live EventsGarcia sent letters this week directing members of Trump's family and top administration officials to preserve documents. Scharf sought to dismiss the requests, noting in a letter to Democratic lawmakers that they are not yet in the majority and cannot compel compliance.Responding to the new executive order, Garcia said Saturday it was part of the administration's "blatant attack on Congress' constitutional right to conduct oversight." He said that despite efforts to impede investigations, "we're just getting started."Rep. Jamie Raskin, the leader of Democratic investigations from the House Judiciary Committee, slammed Trump's order as "totally unprecedented and blatantly unlawful." He said public contractors have a "duty and a right to speak truthfully when Congress calls."In a fact sheet, the White House framed the new requirements as "protecting executive privileges from congressional overreach," arguing that some congressional leaders have tried to intrude on executive branch privileges by "harassing private companies that contract with the federal government."Presidents of both parties have long used executive privilege to resist congressional inquiries, but the claims can set up messy, protracted legal fights as parties dispute whether it applies. Executive privilege allows the president to keep information from the courts, Congress and the public to protect the confidentiality of White House deliberations, but the protection is far from absolute.The latest executive order applies to all contractors and subcontractors, a universe of tens of thousands of businesses.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Nvidia faces US accounting probe amid deepening turmoil — media
news.text: WASHINGTON, United States — US securities regulators are investigating the accounting practices of Nvidia, according to US media, adding to the turmoil engulfing the artificial intelligence chip giant following the resignation of its chief executive.The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) inquiry is in its early stages, The New York Times reported Saturday, citing people briefed on the confidential investigation.The Wall Street Journal reported on the investigation earlier this week, although it was unable to establish its precise focus. The probe could end without any charges being brought against the company.Questions about Nvidia's financial disclosures have intensified amid scrutiny of its dealings with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company investigated by American authorities over suspected shipments of restricted AI chips to China.Nvidia last year changed how it reported sales by geographical location, switching from customers' billing addresses to the countries where they are headquartered, US media reported.The change removed Singapore from its geographical breakdown, despite the company's significant business there.It remains unclear whether the SEC investigation is connected to those accounting changes or to the scandal surrounding former chief executive Jensen Huang.Huang resigned earlier this month following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive suspected by US intelligence of working for Beijing.China has denied the espionage allegations, while Megaspeed has maintained that it operates lawfully.Nvidia's board has appointed former chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO and launched an investigation into the circumstances surrounding Huang's departure.The upheaval has shaken investor confidence in one of the world's most valuable companies, whose advanced semiconductors have been central to the global AI boom.Nvidia shares plunged 14 percent on Friday, bringing their losses for the week to more than 20 percent.US President Donald Trump nevertheless called Friday for Huang to be reinstated.'I think that I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance,' Trump told reporters.But Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones has ruled out his return, saying board directors unanimously accepted his resignation.
news.author: Agence France-Presse

news.title: Schumer and Van Hollen seek support in 13-member incoming class
news.text:
Chuck Schumer and Chris Van Hollen are seeking support from new Democratic senators who campaigned on change ahead of a Dec. 1 secret-ballot vote for Senate Democratic leader, with several still uncommitted.

The 13 Democrats entering the Senate form the largest incoming class in decades, including several who won Republican strongholds after pledging to shake up Washington. Schumer has headed the Senate Democratic caucus since 2017.

The Hill's whip list found 16 senators publicly supporting Schumer as of Nov. 19, while six backed Van Hollen, including himself, and 34 were undecided. Victory requires 28 votes.

Democrats picked up nine Senate seats in the midterms. Before Van Hollen announced his challenge, Aipac congratulated Schumer and incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries on their caucuses' election-night wins.

Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico has called for "new blood" in the party. In a CBS interview two days after the Nov. 3 election, he said he would meet the leadership candidates and ask "tough questions," though he stopped short of rejecting Schumer.

Nevada Sen. Jacky Rosen backed Schumer on X on Nov. 13, writing that he "did the work to deliver what will soon be a 56-seat Senate majority against all odds."

I’ve seen up close how hard @SenSchumer works for our entire caucus. He did the work to deliver what will soon be a 56-seat Senate majority against all odds, and I know he has the experience and the fight to continue leading our diverse caucus at this crucial moment. I’m proud to— Senator Jacky Rosen (@SenJackyRosen) November 13, 2026

That day, Minnesota Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan sought "new voices in our leadership" on social media and pledged her vote to Van Hollen. Oregon Sen. Jeff Merkley endorsed Van Hollen on X.

Americans are desperate to restore government by and for the people, not the privileged and powerful.We need leadership that carries that responsibility in their heart and gut.@ChrisVanHollen is that leader. I've seen him rally support for the people against the powerful time— Senator Jeff Merkley (@SenJeffMerkley) November 13, 2026

Sen. John Fetterman raised a different concern in a Nov. 14 Fox News interview, saying Van Hollen's Israel position could lead him to leave the Democratic Party if Van Hollen became majority leader.

South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews said during a Nov. 17 press call that she had made "no decision" and that "the generational change is represented by this incredibly dynamic incoming freshman class of senators."

At a Schumer news conference on Nov. 18, several activists shouted "Step down, Schumer!" from a distance. Last week, dozens of Sunrise Movement protesters were arrested outside his Washington office after calling on him to "step up or step aside," The Guardian reported.

Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, a moderate considering a presidential bid, announced her choice in an online video on Nov. 19. "Because I’ve been clear that I wasn’t supporting Schumer, I will be supporting Chris Van Hollen," she said.

Slotkin has criticized some of Van Hollen's more progressive policies, a sign of the contest crossing the party's ideological divisions, according to The Associated Press. Kansas Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton said the same day that he would not support Schumer, though he declined to endorse another candidate.

Recruiting and Israel policy

Ohio Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown backs Schumer, who recruited him to run again after he lost his seat in 2024. Schumer oversees the Senate Democrats' campaign spending group, which sent millions into many races, and helped recruit Alaska Sen.-elect Mary Peltola and Roy Cooper.

Schumer took a different course in the primaries involving Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, Flanagan and Maine Sen.-elect Troy Jackson. He backed their opponents before supporting all three nominees, the AP reported.

Van Hollen has pledged to take a more confrontational approach to President Donald Trump, and he backs Medicare for All and ending the filibuster.

Andrews, a 46-year-old pediatrician, became South Carolina's first Democratic Senate winner in nearly three decades. She has sought "generational change" and ruled out supporting Schumer, but she has rejected policies Van Hollen favors, including Medicare for All.

Hamilton became the first Democratic senator from Kansas in nearly a century and called Schumer "a polarizing figure" during his campaign.

The leadership rivals differ on Israel. Schumer, the highest-ranking Jewish elected official in U.S. history, said in 2025 that his "job" is to "keep the left pro-Israel." He has repeatedly described himself as "Shomer Yisrael," or "guardian of Israel."

Schumer has repeatedly opposed measures to limit military aid and weapons sales to Israel during the war in Gaza, although he has supported sanctions on individual settlers.

Van Hollen has voted to block weapons sales to Israel and supports sanctions. He advocates for families of U.S. citizens killed by Israeli soldiers and settlers.

Van Hollen accused Schumer of having "joined with Aipac and crypto" to try to defeat El-Sayed, The Guardian reported. Schumer's office did not respond to a request for comment from The Guardian. Schumer backed Haley Stevens, El-Sayed's Aipac-backed primary opponent, but supported El-Sayed in the general election.

Pressure on senators

MoveOn and Indivisible have endorsed Van Hollen, while calls urging senators to reject Schumer have flooded many of their offices. "Our members are tired of politicians content with incrementalism," MoveOn executive director Joel Payne said.

Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, a Schumer supporter, said, "When the manager takes you to the World Series, you give him another contract."

Brad Parker, associate director of policy at the Center for Constitutional Rights, told The Guardian that "incumbents who ignore the overwhelming and shifting electorate demands to end US complicity in Israeli crimes operate at their own peril."

The Jewish Democratic Council of America endorsed Schumer. "Jewish Americans have been a critical component of a winning Democratic coalition, including in the 2026 midterms," CEO Halie Soifer said.

Earlier this year, 103 House Democrats voted to reduce military aid to Israel, fewer than half of the party's caucus.

The Guardian noted that the Senate leader can broadly set legislative priorities but would not necessarily be able to influence individual votes or foreign policy, particularly for the rest of Trump's term. The paper said the contest has raised Van Hollen's national profile as a Palestinian rights advocate, regardless of the result.

Van Hollen says he has a "path" to victory and has suggested that 15 colleagues will vote for him. The Guardian reported that only five have pledged their support publicly: El-Sayed, Merkley, Bernie Sanders, Flanagan and Slotkin.

Schumer's allies are discussing holding the leadership election earlier, The Hill reported. Schumer, a fifth-term senator, has not said whether his term ending in 2028 will be his last.
news.summary: The incoming class of 13 Democrats is the largest in decades, and several members remain uncommitted ahead of the secret ballot.

news.title: Republicans’ US midterm defeat corners J.D. Vance as 2028 field widens
news.text:
WASHINGTON – A generational defeat in the US midterm elections has left Republicans reeling, with little time to regroup and an expanding field of potential candidates vying to be the party’s presidential nominee in 2028.

Few GOP leaders were hit harder on Election Day than Vice-President J.D. Vance.

Long seen as the likely successor to Donald Trump, Vance is on the defensive as he attempts to balance his fealty to the president and the MAGA base while putting some distance between himself and a leader whose approval rating hovers near 37%.

It’s not going well so far. 

Party strategists anticipate that the field of 2028 aspirants could be far wider than what was expected at the start of the administration, when Trump joked about seeking a constitutionally-barred third term.

Lawmakers who had previously ruled out running now say they are giving it a second thought. 

“J.D. Vance walked into the midterms as a clear frontrunner, but I believe the race to now be wide open,” said Republican strategist Brian Darling.

Former New Orleans mayor Mitch Landrieu, a Democrat, echoed that thought, saying the election “scrambled the playing field pretty dramatically.” 

The day after Republican majorities in the House and Senate were wiped out, Vance’s postmortem pinned the blame squarely on the Iran war – drawing a mild public rebuke from Trump.

Privately, some people familiar with the matter said the president was annoyed by Vance’s statement, though he downplayed the speculation on Nov 20, asserting he didn’t say he was “unhappy with it” and “there’s no problem there at all.”

The perception that Vance has been bruised – and the possibility that Trump won’t anoint him as his heir – is turning the spotlight toward several potential rivals, starting with Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

It was Rubio, travelling with Trump in Asia this week, who was asked to deliver the administration’s response to a domestic crisis: the wave of technology disruptions that have alarmed many Americans. 

From Manila to Shenzhen, as Rubio stood by Trump’s side, a drumbeat of stories buoying his MAGA bona fides and undercutting Vance’s standing with the movement emerged.

“He has a remarkable resume and a compelling backstory as the son of Cuban immigrants, and he has been the absolute superstar of the Trump Cabinet,” said Mark Weaver, a Republican political strategist. 

Trump said on Nov 21 that Vance and Rubio are both popular, but there could be some surprises ahead in the coming months.

“In another few weeks, it’s going to be starting hot and heavy,” Trump said in an interview on Fox News’s Saturday in America. “But remember, we’ve got two years and two months, actually, if you think, and that’s a long time. That’s an eternity in Trump world.”

Others argue that the scale of the GOP defeat gives an edge to contenders from outside the administration.

After the election, Florida governor Ron DeSantis pointed to his state’s red firewall that held despite a wave of Democratic victories across the South – a not-so-subtle hint that he’s best qualified to lead the party as Trump’s political career sunsets. 

During nearly eight years as Florida’s governor, which included a failed 2024 primary challenge to Trump, DeSantis enacted several MAGA policy priorities that he can tout on the campaign trail, including cracking down on businesses employing undocumented immigrants and banning lessons on diversity, equity and inclusion in higher education. 

“DeSantis will be the one who can say he’s really like Trump, but without all of Trump’s baggage,” said Mike DuHaime, a Republican strategist who worked on presidential campaigns for George W. Bush, John McCain, Rudy Giuliani and Chris Christie.

As for a possible DeSantis run, no final decision has been made, according to people familiar with the matter. 

Then there’s Texas Senator Ted Cruz, the last competitor to Trump at the end of the 2016 presidential primaries.

He said on a pre-election podcast that it’s “no secret that I want to be president” and urged his party to ditch the administration’s tariff policy and return to “real free-market” conservatism.

He also disparaged Trump’s vow to send US$5,000 (S$6,447) cheques to Americans if Republicans won, calling it “right-wing socialism.”

Another name tossed around by party officials and donors is Arkansas governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders.

A former White House press secretary in Trump’s first term, Sanders remains a trusted name among both MAGA faithful and the broader GOP establishment.

Her moves to expand access to charter schools, cut state income taxes and tighten sentencing laws for violent offenders have bolstered her standing. 

“People here in Washington sometimes get trapped in a bubble,” said Senator Jim Justice of West Virginia. “It would be natural for her to have a better pulse of the people than the folks here.”

Sanders left open the possibility of a presidential run during a conversation with CNN on Nov 22.

She has also crisscrossed the country promoting a new book, a staple for prospective candidates testing their message before the next election.

Still, other Republican names being floated include Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri, Arkansas Senator Tom Cotton, former Virginia Governor Glenn Youngkin and Senator Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania, though many cautioned that they remain long shots. 

“We got our butts kicked,” McCormick said on Fox News this week.

“I still think we haven’t had adequate conversations about accountability for what went wrong from the commander-in-chief to the leaders of this House and the Senate, to individual senators like me.” 

Hawley, who once ruled out a run, left the door open this week, telling NBC that he was “alarmed by the results of the election.”

Vance’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the emerging 2028 race. 

Just over a year until the first primaries, the cast of potential candidates underscores the party’s disarray. And alarm bells are ringing. 

“It remains to be seen whether President Trump’s policies will have a positive impact on affordability,” said Senator Cynthia Lummis of Wyoming. “It may kick in by 2028, but if it doesn’t, we sure as heck better have a response.”

In the meantime, the hits keep coming for Vance. 

After his critique of the war, Trump pulled him out of negotiations to resolve the conflict and directed him to focus on domestic issues.

Then on Nov 18, Vance abruptly cancelled an appearance at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit after being called back to Washington for meetings on the breakdowns that plagued US tech and aviation industries.

Vance and Trump’s relationship remains strong following the vice-president’s comments about the war, according to a source familiar with the matter. 

His closest political advisers are confident he will still run and that his timeline to make a decision sometime next spring hasn’t changed, the person said, calling speculation that Vance could decide to run in Ohio for governor or a US Senate seat laughable.

A second person also said that Vance hasn’t made up his mind on a presidential candidacy. 

“He needs to run and try and ride out the next two years and hope that the Iran war ends quickly, gas prices come down and there’s some economic relief for what tariffs have done to the economy,” said Darling, the GOP strategist. 

Vance and Rubio flanked Trump at a news conference on Nov 20.

While the president denied any unhappiness with Vance’s statement about the election, he again criticised his vice-president for not saying that going to war was the right decision. 

When Vance was pressed on the issue, his response underscored the conundrum he faces. 

“The president is the one who makes the decision,” Vance said. “And the president has said he would do it again. And my view is that my goal is and my job is to support the president of the United States.” BLOOMBERG
news.author: The Straits Times

news.title: Trump asks fed contractors to consult White House before answering Congress inquiries
news.text: US President Donald Trump has directed federal contractors and subcontractors to consult his administration before responding to inquiries from Congress and withhold information that the White House considers protected by executive privilege.Under a new executive order issued late Friday, companies must coordinate with the White House and federal agencies on “appropriate responses” to congressional requests, with non-compliance potentially resulting in the termination of their government contracts and suspension from future federal work.The order applies to tens of thousands of businesses working as federal contractors and subcontractors. It marks the Trump administration's latest move to restrict how information is shared with Congress ahead of January, when Democrats are set to take control of the legislature and are expected to intensify scrutiny of the administration, AP reported.Democrats have identified federal contracts as a major target for investigations, pointing to the flow of government funds to companies linked to Trump's family, particularly through the Pentagon.White House tightens control over congressional inquiriesThe executive order follows steps by White House officials to exercise greater control over how government agencies and officials handle congressional requests.Trump's counsel, Will Scharf, told federal agencies on Monday that they must obtain approval from his office and the White House's Office of Legislative Affairs before agreeing to appear before Congress, AP reported.In a recent letter to representative Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, Scharf also suggested that some congressional investigations could amount to “blatant criminality”.Garcia had sent letters this week asking members of Trump's family and senior administration officials to preserve documents. Scharf sought to dismiss the requests, arguing that Democrats were not yet in the congressional majority and therefore could not compel compliance.Reacting to the executive order on Saturday, Garcia described it as part of the administration's “blatant attack on Congress’ constitutional right to conduct oversight”. He added that despite efforts to obstruct investigations, “we're just getting started.”Representative Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat leading investigations on the House Judiciary Committee, also criticised the order, calling it “totally unprecedented and blatantly unlawful”. He said government contractors had a “duty and a right to speak truthfully when Congress calls”.White House cites executive privilegeIn a fact sheet, the White House described the new requirements as a measure to protect executive privilege from congressional overreach. It accused some congressional leaders of attempting to intrude on executive branch privileges by “harassing private companies that contract with the federal government”.Presidents from both parties have historically invoked executive privilege to resist congressional inquiries. However, such claims can lead to prolonged legal disputes over whether the protection applies in specific cases.Executive privilege allows a president to withhold certain information from Congress, courts and the public to preserve the confidentiality of White House deliberations, although the protection is not absolute.You use AI every day. news.summary: Federal contractors are now required to coordinate with the White House before responding to congressional inquiries. Non-compliance with the new directive may result in termination of government contracts. This order is part of Trump's effort to limit congressional oversight before Democrats take control. Congressional leaders have criticised the move as an attack on their constitutional rights. The White House claims this measure protects executive privilege from congressional overreach.

news.title: Nvidia faces US accounting probe as Jensen Huang exit, China spy saga deepen turmoil: Report
news.text:
APThe SEC is investigating Nvidia's accounting practices amid scrutiny of its Megaspeed dealings and geographical sales disclosures, adding to investor concerns following Jensen Huang's resignation and a sharp fall in the company's shares.

Washington: US securities regulators are investigating the accounting practices of Nvidia, according to US media, adding to the turmoil engulfing the artificial intelligence chip giant following the resignation of its chief executive.The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) inquiry is in its early stages, The New York Times reported Saturday, citing people briefed on the confidential investigation.The Wall Street Journal reported on the investigation earlier this week, although it was unable to establish its precise focus. The probe could end without any charges being brought against the company.Questions about Nvidia's financial disclosures have intensified amid scrutiny of its dealings with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company investigated by American authorities over suspected shipments of restricted AI chips to China.Nvidia last year changed how it reported sales by geographical location, switching from customers' billing addresses to the countries where they are headquartered, US media reported.Live EventsThe change removed Singapore from its geographical breakdown, despite the company's significant business there.It remains unclear whether the SEC investigation is connected to those accounting changes or to the scandal surrounding former chief executive Jensen Huang.Huang resigned earlier this month following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive suspected by US intelligence of working for Beijing.China has denied the espionage allegations, while Megaspeed has maintained that it operates lawfully.Nvidia's board has appointed former chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO and launched an investigation into the circumstances surrounding Huang's departure.The upheaval has shaken investor confidence in one of the world's most valuable companies, whose advanced semiconductors have been central to the global AI boom.Nvidia shares plunged 14 percent on Friday, bringing their losses for the week to more than 20 percent.US President Donald Trump nevertheless called Friday for Huang to be reinstated."I think that I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance," Trump told reporters.But Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones has ruled out his return, saying board directors unanimously accepted his resignation.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Abdul El-Sayed catches Trump’s attention with pitch for ‘Trumpcare’
news.text: President Donald Trump responded on Saturday to Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed’s push for universal healthcare after the progressive Michigan Democrat pitched that it be called “Trumpcare.” “Donald, this is on the table,” El-Sayed wrote in a post on X last week. “Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.” El-Sayed, a former public health official who made Medicare for All a cornerstone of his campaign, included mock images of “Trumpcare” cards in the post. The cards are branded with the title named after the president and are golden, an homage to Trump’s favorite color. Trump reposted a screenshot of El-Sayed’s post on Truth Social Saturday, though he didn’t include any text with it. However, he said in a phone interview with Fox News earlier in the day that he believes the government could “do tremendous things on healthcare” after Democrats take control of Congress in January. “They have some good points on healthcare, and they have some bad points, and we have some good things, and probably they would say we have some bad things,” Trump said, referring to congressional Democrats. “But there’s a chance we could get great healthcare and a lot of other things, and we do it in a bipartisan way.” Trump also told reporters at a press conference Friday that he is “open to great healthcare.” “There’s a real possibility that we get a lot of great things done, especially on healthcare,” he said. “It can be a combination of what we all want, and we could end up with great healthcare in our country. We could end up better than dealing with the Republicans.” Despite touting his openness to work with Democrats, Trump has also repeatedly emphasized his power to veto legislation since Republican losses in the midterms. “I’ll get along, probably, with the Democrats unless they want to be destructive,” Trump said the day after the election. “But I have the power of the veto.” Trump did say in the interview with Fox News on Saturday that he does not think that vetoing “everything” passed by Democrats for the next two years is the way to go. But he also posted another image of himself on Truth Social later in the day, showing him in a red “VETO”-branded hat and a matching jacket. In a statement Saturday afternoon, El-Sayed said he is “happy to chat” with the president if his intentions to work together on healthcare are genuine. “If the President is serious about meeting the unmet promise of guaranteed healthcare in this country, I’m ready to work alongside leaders in the Senate like Senators Van Hollen, Sanders, Wyden, and Warren to deliver,” El-Sayed said. “President Trump, give me a call.”

news.title: Ballistic missile attack on Zelenskyy’s hometown in central Ukraine kills 2 and wounds dozens
news.text: KYIV, Ukraine — A Russian strike on the center of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s hometown, Kryvyi Rih, killed two people and wounded 60 others, local officials said Saturday. Meanwhile, a Russian cargo ship bound for Kaliningrad caught fire in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday after it was hit by drones, Finnish and Russian officials said. It was not clear who struck the ship not far from the Russian border. The Finnish prime minister warned that the war was spilling into the region. A 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman were killed in the attack Friday night on Kryvyi Rih in central Ukraine, Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of the city administration, wrote on Telegram. Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the regional military administration, said 60 people were wounded, including six children. The strike caused four fires and damaged about 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools and an industrial facility, as well as businesses and vehicles, Vilkul said. Video footage published by the regional branch of the Ukrainian State Emergency Service appeared to show further strikes while ambulance and firefighting crews were responding at the scene, as fires burned around them. “First, two ballistic missiles. And then, when the emergency and rescue operation began, three more rockets hit doctors, rescuers and utility workers,” Vilkul wrote on Telegram. The attack added to uncertainty about the prospects for ongoing talks brokered by Washington. It also came hours after two Russian missiles and a suspected drone came down in Poland, in what its prime minister said was likely a provocation timed to coincide with European military exercises in his country. In the unprecedented two-week military exercise that began Nov. 9 in southeastern Poland, forces are preparing for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine aimed at helping to stabilize the country and rebuild its military. European countries previously have expressed alarm at what they deem to be Russia’s attempts to destabilize the continent. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, speaking to reporters in Warsaw on Saturday, called the airspace violation “dangerous” and said all allies stood “in full solidarity with Poland.” “NATO will defend every inch of Polish territory,” Rutte said. He said the alliance functioned “as it should” on Friday morning, when NATO jets supported Polish F-16s scrambled as Russian objects approached Polish airspace. NATO’s top military commander was assessing the alliance’s defenses and would make adjustments if needed, Rutte said. Crimean Bridge strikes ‘fair response,’ Zelenskyy says At a meeting with U.K. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting in Kyiv, Zelenskyy said Saturday that Ukraine’s repeated attacks on the Kerch Bridge linking occupied Crimea with the Russian mainland were a “fair response” to scores of Russian attacks on Ukrainian bridges. He said that Russia President Vladimir Putin had “attacked Ukrainian bridges 109 times.” “Not the number of missiles — the number of attacks,” he said. “This is important, that’s why it’s our absolutely fair response.” The Ukrainian leader said Putin “doesn’t want to stop the war” and is looking to escalate. He also rejected Putin’s claim that the Kerch bridge is used exclusively by civilian traffic. “If he can use internet, he can use it and see tanks, armored vehicles, artillery,” the Ukrainian leader said. Streeting called the airspace violations in Poland “an outrageous provocation” and urged allies to respond by stepping up support for Ukraine. “The more they try and deter Europe from supporting Ukraine, the more we will step up,” he said. Zelenskyy reacts to Trump calling Putin his friend The drone incursion in Poland stoked tensions between Europe and Moscow just as the U.S. tries to add momentum to talks it is mediating on ending the war that began with Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine nearly five years ago. U.S. President Donald Trump discussed the war with Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at a summit in China on Thursday, according to his envoy Steve Witkoff. Trump called Putin his “friend” during the meeting and continued to tout their relationship at a White House news conference Friday. Asked about Trump’s remarks in an interview with CNN, Zelenskyy called Putin “a killer.” “For us, he is an enemy. And of course, for us, he is a killer,” Zelenskyy said Friday. He warned that describing the Russian leader in friendly terms could mean “he doesn’t feel enough pressure.” Russian cargo ship is on fire in the Gulf of Finland Two drones attacked the vessel in “neutral waters” 3 nautical miles from the Russian border, Alexander Drozdenko, the governor of Russia’s Leningrad region, wrote on Telegram. He later said the crew had not needed to be evacuated and that the situation on board was “under control,” with preparations being made for the vessel to resume navigation. The ship drifted into Finnish territorial waters, the Finnish Border Guard said in a statement, adding that it posed no danger to maritime traffic. Finnish border guards were carrying out a rescue operation and preparing for possible environmental damage, it said. According to a statement sent to Estonian media, Estonian authorities received a report that a fire had broken out on the Russian cargo ship Sparta II, which was sailing in the Gulf of Finland. The ship had drifted out of Estonia’s exclusive economic zone earlier Saturday. According to preliminary reports, explosions occurred on board. “War is spilling into our immediate vicinity,” Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo wrote on X. Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea, between Poland and Lithuania. Finland’s Defense Ministry also said that a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating Finnish airspace around noon Saturday, flying about 2.5 miles into the country. Defense Minister Antti Häkkänen said the incident may have been related to rescue or monitoring operations involving the damaged ship. Elsewhere in Ukraine, 11 people, including two children, were wounded when a Russian drone attacked a five-story apartment building in the Kharkiv region, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said Saturday. One person was wounded in a Russian attack on the capital, Kyiv, according to the service. In Russia, local officials said Saturday that Ukrainian drone attacks wounded three people in the Bryansk and Belgorod border regions.
