news.title: Diehard eyepatched January 6 leader who has tattoo of Donald Trump says he's 'absolutely done' with president and calls him a 'traitor'
news.text:
A man who once tattooed Donald Trump on his arm and played a prominent role in the January 6 Capitol riot says he's fully turned on the President whom he now calls a 'traitor.' 

Stewart Rhodes even received a commutation for his 18-year prison sentence after he was convicted of seditious conspiracy when Trump returned to office in 2025. 

'I am absolutely done with Trump,' said Rhodes, sitting at a rickety yellow table outside a gastropub in Irving, Texas. 

He considers Trump not just a traitor, but 'one of the very worst in our nation's history.'

The repudiation from a former acolyte is another example of how allegiance to the president has faded even among extreme supporters. 

Back then, Rhodes claimed Trump lost the 2020 White House race to Democrat Joe Biden because of election fraud. 

This year in Texas, where Democrats had historic victories, he said there's another reason.

'The lion's share is because Trump pissed off his own base,' Rhodes said, his face shaded by a black cowboy hat. 

An eye patch covers his left socket, the result of an old gun accident, and a glacial blue iris peers out from the other.

Nearby, people mingled with drinks for his Christian Warriors After-Party, organized during a three-day conference called 'Christ is King: America After Trump.' 

Some people approached to shake hands or sign up for the Oath Keepers or trainings for things like community defense and hurricane relief.

The beginning of Rhodes' break with Trump came when the President gave pardons to hundreds of people who were locked up for their actions on January 6, 2021, but only commuted Rhodes' sentence. 

'That was the first inkling,' Rhodes said.

Rhodes also said Trump's war with Iran violated Trump's promises to end foreign conflicts. 

And, Rhodes said, it felt like an affront when Trump dismissed people who urged his administration to release files about the Jeffrey Epstein case, calling them 'PAST supporters.' 

Then Rhodes felt Trump went back on his longtime slogan.

'We elected him to end the corruption in Washington, DC. ''Drain the swamp.'' Unfortunately his administration has been one of the most corrupt administrations in U.S. history,' Rhodes said. 

'The pardons are pay-for-play and everything is pay-for-play.'

The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

Rhodes is not alone in his about-face on Trump, but there's an ideological through line, said Sam Jackson, an associate professor at the University at Albany with a focus on anti-government extremism.

'They went from seeing Donald Trump as their ally in this fight against the conspiracy, to actually being co-opted by the conspiracy,' Jackson said, and it 'points to deeper consistency in that understanding of the world as driven by hidden, evil actors.'

Rhodes, who graduated from Yale Law School and worked for Ron Paul, founded the Oath Keepers in 2009 with the goal of encouraging members of the military and law enforcement to resist what they view as unconstitutional orders, such as disarming citizens or carrying out warrantless searches.

Rhodes later allied himself with Trump's political movement, and the Oath Keepers supported his attempt to remain in office after losing the 2020 election. 

Fueled by conspiracies about voter fraud, prosecutors said group members gathered weapons, organized trainings and assembled in Washington, where some helped storm the Capitol on January 6.

Rhodes, who did not enter the building that day, said he was a 'political prisoner' who faced 'illegality' in his trial. 

He was sentenced to 18 years, one of the longest sentences of any January 6-related case.

'You are smart, you are charismatic and compelling and frankly that´s what makes you dangerous,' US District Judge Amit Mehta said during the hearing. 

'The moment you are released, whenever that may be, you will be ready to take up arms against your government.'

Rhodes was behind bars as Trump began his political comeback. 

He said he watched the assassination attempt in Butler on a prison television with other inmates. 

Rhodes saw Trump pump his fist and yell 'fight,' and he figured that God´s hand was on the man.

After Trump won the 2024 election, he swiftly pardoned hundreds of people convicted of crimes related to January 6, including those who assaulted police officers. 

Rhodes received a commutation, which didn´t wipe his record clean.

'He let us out of prison. We were grateful. I didn't get a pardon though,' he said.

The Justice Department vacated Rhodes's conviction earlier this year, lifting his felon status. 

Rhodes said he's working to rebuild the Oath Keepers, which previously had tens of thousands of members, according to leaked lists. W

ith his rights restored, Rhodes said his first priority was to get some guns, and he didn't register to vote in time for the election. 

But he said he wouldn't have cast a ballot anyway.

That's because Rhodes felt that 'the Republican Party has taken us for granted,' and he didn't want to choose between 'a half a dose of poison or a full dose.'

As for his tattoo of Trump, the man he now considers a traitor, Rhodes has plans that he didn't specify.

'I will have this prison tattoo of Trump `modified,'' he wrote in a text message, 'to reflect that reality. That treason.
news.summary: Stewart Rhodes received a commutation for his 18-year prison sentence after he was convicted of seditious conspiracy when Trump returned to office in 2025.
news.author: Editor,Stephen M. Lepore

news.title: Labor pushes back on Trump data centre tax threat
news.text: Labor has bristled at Donald Trump's pledge to put a "tremendous tax" on US companies building data centres overseas. The US president issued the warning on his return from the APEC summit in China, where the battle between Washington and Beijing over what Mr Trump terms "super intelligence" loomed large. Canberra views data centre investment in Australia as crucial to securing home-grown artificial intelligence capability, but Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles argued it was also in the US's best interests. "If all of that infrastructure is in one place - in other words, if it remains solely in the United States, right there, there's a vulnerability," he told ABC's Insiders on Sunday. "What's in the interests of the United States itself is that they do build redundancy beyond the United States in respect of this tech, and Australia, we think, has a significant role to play." Mr Trump did not provide further details for his tax plans, but he said the US would "fight very hard for the data centres" to prevent China winning the AI development race. But Mr Marles said internationalising AI infrastructure was at the heart of the "pax silica" declaration the US, Australia, the European Union and 24 other countries signed in December 2025, with the notable exclusion of China. It calls on signatories to reduce excessive dependencies and work together to build a trustworthy supply chain for the technology. "In the fullness of time, the importance of being able to have redundant infrastructure outside of the United States, the imperative of that is going to become clear," Mr Marles said. The deputy prime minister's comments come as public opinion on data centres sours over concerns about their water and energy demands, as well as their carbon footprint. A report released on Thursday showed nine proposed data centres could produce as much pollution as the nation's three dirtiest coal-fired power stations if allowed to operate without renewable energy requirements. ASIO director-general Mike Burgess has also warned data centres are equal parts "hype, opportunity and threat" in an interview with Nine newspapers, saying foreign powers could use the infrastructure as a way of controlling sensitive technology and information. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said the government was alive to the threat. "Whenever you get that sort of capability onshore, it also becomes a magnet for people who would want to conduct foreign interference," he told News24. "We need to make sure that we are alert and that we are being very careful in the ownership structures that happen in Australia for data centres." While not commenting directly on the US president's proposed foreign data centre tax, Mr Burke stressed cooperation between the US and Australia on AI benefited both countries. "Having data centres in Australia, there's a national security interest in being able to do it," he said. Labor is still mulling over national regulations for data centre development with draft legislation expected before the end of the year. Australian Associated Press
news.author: Will Nicholas

news.title: 'They are wrong': Defence minister denies US report on AUKUS submarines
news.text:
Defence Minister Richard Marles has rebuffed reports that the AUKUS agreement to supply nuclear-powered submarines to Australia would diminish the US naval force for "many years". 

Mr Marles also downplayed US President Donald Trump's threats about US artificial intelligence companies building data centres overseas, as well as ASIO boss Mike Burgess's warning about foreign interference within Australia's AI data centre sector.

A report from the US Congressional Budget Office, released on Friday, said "the US submarine industrial base is currently struggling to meet the Navy's demand for submarines".

"Increasing production further to replace SSNs [nuclear-powered submarines] sold to Australia would increase the challenges that the Navy and the shipyards are facing," the report read.

"The sale of SSNs to Australia would reduce the number of attack submarines available to the Navy for many years."

Mr Marles told ABC's Insiders he was not worried about the report and expected many like it over the next decade.

"The reason it doesn't worry me is because AUKUS is very much happening," he said.

He agreed that the production rate of shipbuilding was "definitely a critical part" of Australia getting Virginia class submarines, but denied that the US navy's production rate was flat.

"They're wrong? The US Congressional Office?" Insiders host David Speers asked.

He said the production rate was one factor, but "sustainment and maintenance" were also important to ensure Australia would receive its first Virginia class nuclear submarine by the early 2030s.

"The very first milestone that we have always been shooting for is the establishment of the Submarine Rotational Force — West this time next year," he said, referring to US and UK nuclear-powered boats having a rotational presence at HMAS Stirling, allowing Australian sailors to deploy on those vessels to get experience with naval nuclear propulsion.

"We're well on track to see that occur."

AI data centre fears

US President Donald Trump has said he will not allow American AI companies to build data centres in foreign countries.

Mr Trump warned there would be "tremendous taxes" for those who do.

The comments come amid an AI data centre boom in Australia, where operators have raised a record sum of at least $35 billion as of September this year.

Mr Marles said the government would continue to work with the tech companies themselves and the US government about investment in Australia, adding it was in their own interests.

"If all of that infrastructure is in one place, in other words, if it remains solely in the United States, right there, there's a vulnerability," he said.

"And that's partly why they are looking abroad and why we are of such interest.

"We would like to see that investment in Australia. Of course, you know, it's not at any cost. We need to be doing it on our terms."

Australia this week signed a US-led agreement to identify vulnerable supply chains and protect sensitive AI technology from theft or foreign interference.

Mr Marles said that agreement also encouraged AI data centres to be built overseas.

ASIO boss Mike Burgess has also issued a warning about foreign interference, telling 60 Minutes that foreign actors building AI data centres here may try to access sensitive information or critical infrastructure covertly.

Mr Marles says "it is a concern".

"This is the world that we live in, so in a sense it's not new, but the building of data centres creates a new vector, a new avenue for foreign actors to engage in," he said.

"But we are very mindful of our own cyber security."

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said there was a "national security" interest in Australia housing AI data centres, and referred to Mr Burgess's comments that it came with both opportunity and risk.

"Whenever you get that sort of capability on shore, it also becomes a magnet for people who would want to conduct foreign interference," Mr Burke told News24.

"So we need to make sure that we are alert and that we are being very careful in the ownership structures that happen in Australia for data centres."
news.summary: Defence Minister Richard Marles rebuffs reports that the AUKUS agreement to supply nuclear-powered submarines to Australia would diminish the US naval force for "many years".
news.author: Erin Handley

news.title: Trump hints at ‘four or five’ finalists for White House press secretary after telling Katie Zacharia ‘you don’t need this’
news.text:
President Donald Trump suggested in a Fox News interview Saturday that he was considering “four or five” finalists for White House press secretary.

Trump also defended Katie Zacharia, who was fired after just five days in the role following a widely panned debut briefing. The position has remained vacant since her October 16 ouster.

During the interview, host Kayleigh McEnany asked, “Do you think we’ll know who the new press secretary is before the new year?”

“Well, I have four or five people,” Trump, speaking by phone, responded. “I can tell you I have a hundred people that want that job as you can imagine. OK? A hundred people.”

He added: “We had one who’s a very good person, Katie. She’s a fantastic person ... But I saw the way she was being treated. I said, ‘Katie you don’t need this.’”

Zacharia, a former Newsmax commentator, drew criticism from Democrats and Republicans after her 14-minute debut briefing, during which she took questions from just three journalists and mistakenly referred to her husband as “my president.” 

She also faced scrutiny for describing herself as a lawyer despite never passing a bar exam, and is now under investigation by the State Bar of California.

“She might’ve been able to fight her way out of it,” Trump continued. “But why should she be put in that position? ‘Cause I think she might’ve actually been very good. But I said ‘what do you need this for?’”

He continued: “They really came at her. I was surprised to see it. Nasty. So maybe that’s over with now and somebody else would come in and they’ll be a little bit more normalized.”

After her ouster, Zacharia defended her performance, saying she was not given enough time to prepare. Asked by The Free Press this week whether she would take the job again, she responded: “There’s just no way that I would say no to that man.”

Names floated among political analysts as potential new hires in recent weeks include Danielle Alvarez, a former senior adviser to Trump’s 2024 campaign, and Deputy Press Secretary Anna Kelly.

Earlier this month, Trump also offered the job to UFC president and CEO Dana White, who declined. Trump later said he had been joking.

Zacharia’s predecessor, Karoline Leavitt, served as the president’s chief spokesperson for 19 months before leaving in August to spend more time with her family.

Trump had four press secretaries during his first term: Sean Spicer, Sarah Huckabee Sanders, Stephanie Grisham and McEnany, who is now a Fox News personality.
news.summary: ‘I can tell you I have a hundred people that want that job as you can imagine,’ Trump told Fox News
news.author: Brendan Rascius
